items.title: Being Wife of Dancing Governor: ‘What I discovered about the Adeleke family’
items.description: By Morenike Taire While tribal relations in Southern Nigeria have deteriorated of late, many marriages between Yorubas and Igbos continue to thrive in all strata of society. Notable of such unions is the one between the executive governor of the state of Osun, Prince Ademola Adeleke, and his Imo born wife, Ngozi. The Osun First lady lived in the South West for the first time as a youth corp member serving with the now defunct Societe Generale Bank, having schooled up to Masters level in the East. As fate would have it, she was retained at the bank’s Dugbe, Ibadan branch and went on to work almost 23 years in the banking industry leaving only in 2018 to support her husband’s political career. The transition for her, was not too difficult. “I miss banking, but what would you have me do? I like being up and doing, facing challenges. A lot was demanded of one, which is the situation I find myself in now. As wife of governor, every time it’s people’s requests, meetings here and there, traveling which I also like. I like meeting people and new things everyday so this situation ushers in a new opportunity. I love helping the downtrodden and being wife of governor has thrown me in the middle of it. Women, widows, people living with disability, so many people to take care of, think of. It gives me joy and happiness”. Her Foundation, Esther Adeleke Foundation, was born out of her challenge in having a child when she got married, drawing her into looking for motherless babies to seek the face of God. According to her, in fact it worked. “Before I touched my salary, I would first credit SOS’s account. From time to time I would gather my friends, go and visit them with materials, foodstuffs and so forth. When my baby clocked one year I told His Excellency that my spirit tells me to go and celebrate her birthday with the children there. A lot of friends refused to come. I had to call all the friends I met in the course of looking for a baby, going from one hospital to another. These children’s faces bring luck. Majority of them that came got their blessing. I recommended them to so many people. When you take up motherless babies, pray along with them they will pray for you”. She revealed to Vanguard that she coped the same way in the political terrain as she coped when working as a banker, adding that banking was even more demanding. “In banking, because then you would sometimes wake up at 4 to dress up and face the road at 6 and sometimes you come back late; but now, yes there are all kinds of back and forth, traveling, but not too much of what I cannot handle”. Like many Nigerians before now, her experience with intertribal marriage has been quite interesting as someone who loves challenges. “I don’t know for others but for me, it has been happy moments everyday. I open my mind to learning their own way of doing things. The only thing I have not learned is how to swallow amala. I cannot stand that one they call ewedu, even the one in my place not to talk of the one made with broom. As for pounded yam, I love it”. She has equally fallen in love with the owambe culture with parties on Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. “The beautiful thing is that when you have a party to plan, even your enemy will buy souvenir. We will do the party, enjoy ourselves, then when we go back home we can continue. Everyone will forget their problems. When I used to work in Lagos Island, they would block the road”. “I so much love the culture generally and they embraced me even before my husband dreamed of becoming a governor. All the women would rush to the car before I come down and surround the car, sing for me, hug me. After becoming the governor’s wife you can imagine how it escalated. Even when I can’t understand, they would sing for me and I would dance. I would ask them what they are saying and they would tell me. I know they cannot say anything bad”. “I have a welcoming attitude. My father told my husband, “I’m allowing this my daughter to marry you because I know she has a good character”. I am enjoying every bit of it”. The question most people want to ask is, what is it about the Adelekes and women from the South East? The First Lady has a bird’s eye view. “Their mother, Esther Nnenna Adeleke is from Abia State. My husband and siblings were all born and bred in Enugu, their father used to work at the military hospital in Enugu. All the extended family were all in Enugu at one time. They all speak Igbo like Igbo people. You will definitely identify with the root of your mother. Their daughters are allowed to marry from anywhere. In Adeleke family, anywhere you find your happiness, go there. They don’t restrict their children wether boys or girls. For them, it’s a free world”. Her husband’s reputation as “the dancing governor”, far from being embarrassing, is something she embraces with pride. “I feel good. My husband did not start dancing today. I got to meet with him when he schooled in the US. They called him Jackson because of his dancing skills. When we went to my village for my traditional marriage, my husband danced from morning till the next morning. He brought Shina Peters himself and another musician. It was like a carnival. I don’t think my village people have ever seen that type of wedding up till today. They still talk about it. I didn’t marry him a politician. Then, his elder brother was the one involved in politics. When he came on board, people were thinking he just started dancing. When my village people now see him on video or television they say, “leave him for us, we appreciate him”. “In my house now, I can say I am the only one that doesn’t know how to dance. If you know my husband, you will not see him sick or angry because at any given time, if he’s not singing he is praising God or dancing. He’s a very strong man, loves people around him, merry making. With him, no dull moment. My husband was in the choir. He can beat the drum, sing very well”, she revealed. Her Foundation, named after her mother in law who passed 12 years ago was born out of a heart for charity, right from a home where the parents liked giving. “My parents would train poor people’s children. My father was a teacher and if he identified any brilliant student that had challenges, my father would bring such a child home and take up the training. My mother, most of the time,5 bought foodstuffs and shared anything shareable”. “Coming in to my husband’s family I discovered they liked to give. Almost half of students in Adeleke University are under the Adeleke scholarship scheme. Same in secondary and primary. The grace of God abounds and they will still take care of their workers. I so much cherish it”. The First Lady is particularly interested in the care of women that deliver triplets in her state, as the birth of triplets seems to be more common amongst couples who are already struggling economically. “God has a way of doing his own things. They cannot even pay their hospital bills not to talk of buying pampers, food and everything. I take them up, pay their bills and keep helping them. Even a woman that delivers just one child needs enough food to produce enough milk, talk less of the one that delivered 3. Sometimes they go into depression which, if not properly managed, goes into mental issues. What I am doing is giving them something for start-up. Even when I am not there I will know the children are okay. The first triplets we had in 2023 are about to start school now and I ask myself, when they want to buy bags and so on, will they be calling me? I will still be monitoring them and supporting them in my own little way too”. The Foundation also does SME and technical training in partnership with pan-African University; as well as train the trainers scheme in Osun University and polytechnics. In addition, she collaborates with Fidelity Food Bank and Adewole Foundation in the US. “We sensitise girls on menstrual hygiene and share pad while educating them on how to navigate goings on in the world”. The First Lady wishes she could wave a magic wand, as finance has been a problem. “It breaks my heart when I don’t have to give. The money which was meant for civil servants is not released. If this government was not prudent enough, you and I know there will be protests and eruptions in the state but he is using his security vote plus y support to pay all the pensioners. They were dying in their dozens. These are people that have served their state. There’s something they used to call afsa (half salary) but the backlog has been cleared and minimum wage is now 75k. What they planned was for my husband to have problems with civil servants. They are happy with Imole’s government. You will miss your way in Osogbo and you will sleep with your two eyes closed. It’s the Grace of God”. “I want to encourage all women to keep mentoring our young girls. You must not bring a child to your home before you can help”, she said. The post Being Wife of Dancing Governor: ‘What I discovered about the Adeleke family’ appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Prince Nico boys conquer Enugu with father’s music, plan African tour
items.description: By Fred Iwenjora Nico Jnr and Phils, two sons of famous musician Prince Nico Mbarga founder of Rocafiljazz band were in Enugu over the last weekend in what many consider a musical conquest of the coal city state. And fans agree that they were victorious in this musical battle. This is in the family’s resolve to continuously work musically to keep their father’s musical heritage and legacies alive. The duo backed up by the reconstituted band brought their father’s panco system brand of highlife music first to Toscana, then at the International conference centre Enugu for an NGO anniversary before capping up at the Davids Hill centre on Saturday night. In the tightly coordinated band, Nico jnr, a master guitarist and singer backs his brother Phils (another multi instrumentalist) lead voice as they reeled out their father’s evergreen songs like Sweet mother, Simplicity, Good father, na my choice, music system, Christiana etc At the end of the 3 days musical onslaught, both Enugu fans and the band were grateful to each other for a strong symbiotic relationship. In a post from the Enugu ICC on Sunday before their departure from Enugu, Nico thanked Enugu people for reception and hospitality. Nico jnr had earlier said that getting older made them realise the legacy they are laden with and started preparing for whatever fans are seeing today. He said “We first went to school before perfecting the songs we grew up with and now we are strictly in performance mode. And no looking back” He further hinted that the band is ever ready for any kinds of invitations. Meanwhile their sister Estelle who is one of the pillars of the Nico Mbarga Sweet Mother Foundation has announced an African tour for the Rocafiljazz band rebirth soonest. According to Estelle, the singer and fashion designer third daughter of Prince Nico, “Rocafil jazz band is here to stay and not going anywhere. “We are on a mission to take our father’s music around the world all over again. Please join us on this ride She dropped the tour plan which includes West, East and Central African countries. Pince Nico was one of the star artistes of Rogers All stars records label whose song Sweet Mother is still one of the best selling African songs of all time He died in a ghastly motor accident on 24 June 1997. He had ten children most of whom are musically inclined. A statue of him is standing at Ikom, Cross River state where he was raised. items.title: NIMR crisis deepens as research professors face premature retirement
items.description: By Ishola Balogun At the Nigerian Institute of Medical Research (NIMR), the corridors once alive with the hum of discovery now echo with uncertainty. Professors and Research Fellows—men and women who have dedicated decades to probing Nigeria’s most pressing health challenges—find themselves staring at eviction notices and premature retirement letters. Their crime? Serving more than eight years as Directors in a system where tenure rules were never meant to apply to them. The dispute stems from the Federal Government’s policy providing for eight-year tenure for Directors in the Federal Public Service. Prof. John Obafunwa, Director-General of NIMR, moved to enforce the Federal Government’s eight-year tenure policy on academic and research cadre Directors. But the union’s position is that the policy was never intended to retire Research/Academic Cadre Directors who are essentially career researchers and professors. The Academic Staff Union of Research Institutions, ASURI points to a definitive clarification issued by the Office of the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation (OHCSF) on November 29, 2014. The clarification, referenced as HCSF/EPO/EIR/RR/6411436T/54 and addressed to the then Minister of Science and Technology, stated: “Officers of Research under the purview of your Ministry who were appointed as Research/Academic Cadre staff, and whose career advancement fulfills the specified conditions, including publications, may continue in service until they attain the age of 65 years in line with the provisions of the extant rules.” The clarification added: “This is without prejudice to the eight- year tenure policy of the government.” To ASURI, that document settled the matter. The union says the clarification established that Research/Academic Cadre staff could remain in service until 65, while the eight-year rule applied to Directors who were not members of the Research/Academic Cadre. A policy misapplied ASURI considered it as a policy misapplied, adding that the eight-year tenure policy was designed for administrative Directors in the Federal Public Service, not for academics whose careers are tied to research and teaching. It stated that multiple clarifications from the Office of the Head of Civil Service of the Federation (OHCSF) over the past two decades exempted research and academic cadre Directors. A 2014 letter explicitly stated: “Officers of Research under the purview of your Ministry who were appointed as Research/Academic Cadre staff… may continue in service until they attain the age of 65 years in line with the provisions of the extant rules.” Yet, despite these clarifications, NIMR’s management pressed forward. Grants were terminated, projects stalled, and professors were told to vacate their offices and residences. Reacting to the development, the Secretary-General of the Academic Staff Union of Research Institutions (ASURI), Prof. Theophilus Ndubuaku said:, “Now you say all the research professors should retire because they have served as directors for eight years.” He was lamenting. “Funny enough, the people they are asking to retire are the ones who mentor the new people. If they go now, the new people will not have mentors, amid a ban on employment.” “You drive a professor out of his residence, and he has not collected his gratuity and pension,” Ndubuaku explained. “Most of them don’t have savings. They are indebted to cooperatives and loans to train their children. You now ask him to pack out. This is the predicament of researchers.” Similar issue in court The crisis deepened in July when the National Industrial Court struck down the Federal Government’s circular enforcing the eight-year tenure rule on education directors. Justice Olufunke Anuwe ruled that teachers and education officers are entitled to remain in service until 65 years of age or 40 years of pensionable service. The court declared the circulars illegal, null, and void, granting a perpetual injunction against their implementation. Though the case was specific to education officers, the principle resonates strongly with research institutes. Both cadres are governed by similar rules, and the judgment reinforces ASURI’s position that research directors cannot be forced out prematurely. For research fellows, the ruling was a beacon of hope. But at NIMR, the management’s stance remained unchanged. The Union’s fury Responding to questions via phone, Prof. Theophilus Ndubuaku, said: “NIMR Chief Executive is insisting because he got a letter from his Ministry that the research professors must go. “For the past twenty years, the HOCSF has maintained through letters that research Directors are not supposed to be affected by the tenure policy. The policy says that if a Director serves for eight years, he should retire. It is public service policy. The Director of research is not just directors, they are professors. About six years ago, we changed their nomenclature to Research Fellows. We wanted research nomenclature different from what is in the public service. Even in the university, the professor is not a Director. And that was approved by the same HOCSF. Now that you are calling them Research Directors is a misnomer. They are Research professors or Research Fellows. So, when you passed a circular that Directors must retire after eight years, it should not affect us especially for the past twenty years, the HOCSF have written dozens of letters to CEOs/DGs that they are exempted from eight- year tenure. “Now the HOCSF now wrote a letter saying Directors who have put in eight years should retire and then, you want to target Research Fellows and Professors, what they are not doing in the university. The law that creates Research Institutions states that Research Institutions should be run outside the public service. This is very clear. So, why do you bring in a public service policy into the research institution especially when you have clarified for twenty years that they are exempted? This is coming just because nobody cares about research; otherwise, what the President should have done was to call the Chief Executives or HOCSF to order just like what he did to EFCC and Osun state government recently. They want to destroy the system, but nobody cares to look at the research thinking it is not productive, whereas, it is what saves any nation. The result of the research does not come out immediately. It is not an industry where you create the result immediately. But it is research that drives industries, drives lives. We saw that during covid-19. Now, look at what Ebola is doing in DRCongo. Any country that is not prepared for such will just pick their citizens on the streets. With what is going on at NIMR now, as the only medical institution in Nigeria, where is our preparation for the next epidemic? Nigeria is in danger. Not just about hunger, it is about our health. It is only when you are alive that you will eat. Prof Ndubuaku said: “We know our fight. The DG of NIMR is pushing us to the wall. If we come and lock that gate tomorrow, he will now say unions are bad, they are radicals. Go and check his records on what he did at LASU” Research at risk For many Research Fellows, the trauma is compounded by the sense of futility. They have labored for decades, often with meager resources, to build Nigeria’s research capacity. Now, at the twilight of their careers, they face eviction and humiliation. “What does a Professor earn? N500,000 a month,” Ndubuaku noted. “They don’t have savings. They are indebted. And you now ask them to go even when they are not up to 60 years of age.” The crisis at NIMR is not just about tenure rules. It is about Nigeria’s future. Research is the backbone of development, yet the country has consistently neglected it. “There is a common knowledge globally that no country can develop without research,” Ndubuaku said. “No amount of borrowing can save us. Nigeria is getting into deeper problems because there must be some form of production to repay the money you are borrowing lest you go bankrupt.” A nation at the bottom “From UNESCO report, we now have 5.4 researchers per million people. A country like Ghana has over 50 researchers per million. Put the two in context and see the difference. How do we catch up as far as development is concerned? All those countries that have 400 are the countries exporting goods to us. This is because they are doing research since you cannot produce without first carrying out research. “Even when you do ‘adopting technology’, or ‘reverse engineering’, you still need to do research. And it is not a motor-park tout that will do reverse engineering, even if you want to steal technology, you cannot steal what you cannot use. So, as we speak now, Nigeria is at the bottom globally. That is when you hear that we are the poverty capital, we are the most insecure country, we have the highest number of poor people below poverty line, and child mortality is high. “Now, you say all the research professors, they should retire because they have served as Directors or Professors for eight years. Funny enough, the people they are asking to retire are the people that will mentor the new people. It means if they go now, the new people will not have mentors, amid ban on employment. The implications are stark. Without research, Nigeria cannot prepare for epidemics. “With what is going on at NIMR now, as the only medical institution in Nigeria, is it where you are going to prepare for the next epidemic? No. Nigeria is in danger,” Ndubuaku warned. “Not just about hunger, it is about our health.” A clash of perspectives Prof. Obafunwa, the man at the center of the storm, has remained largely silent, declining to respond to questions on phone, saying “I don’t grant interviews over the phone.” But his insistence on enforcing the policy has baffled colleagues and enraged unions. “Why can’t the CEO of NIMR wait?” Prof Ndubuaku asked. “If eventually, the government says they don’t care about research, they should go, so be it. But why can’t he just be patient?” Other institutions have chosen a different path. Some CEOs have ignored the circular, relying instead on earlier clarifications that exempted research directors. According to Prof Ndubuaku, they insisted that “Until they now get a circular saying they have withdrawn the exemption of Research Directors, they will not implement.” “But the NIMR CEO is so bent on implementing it,” he said. The risk of collapse If the crisis festers, the consequences could be catastrophic. Research projects will be stalled, international funding may dry up, and Nigeria’s already fragile health system could collapse. “For the past two years, there has not been any research development,” one source at NIMR revealed. “Research professors are hounded, grants were terminated, and no major project carried out under this leadership, traumatizing professors and Research Fellows and creating a hostile working environment for staff.” The trauma is palpable. Professors who once blaze the trail on some medical areas now face eviction. Their contributions, their sacrifices, their dreams, all at risk of being erased by a policy misapplied. Prof Ndubuaku asked: I wonder, why can’t he wait? “If those professors packed out from their houses and you allocated their apartments to junior officers, and at the end, the government now says, ‘Oh, it was a mistake,’ what would you do?”. “Why can’t the CEO of NIMR wait?” Reflection The NIMR crisis is a microcosm of Nigeria’s larger struggle with research and development. It is a story of neglect, mismanagement, and misplaced priorities. But above all, it is a human story, of professors who have given their lives to science, now facing trauma and uncertainty. Their plight is not just about tenure rules; it is about the soul of a nation struggling to find its place in the world. If Nigeria allows its Research Fellows to be cast aside, the cost will be measured not just in careers lost, but in lives. Epidemics will strike, poverty will deepen, and the country will remain at the bottom of every index of development. The professors’ voices are clear: research is not a luxury. It is survival. ASURI’s position ASURI warned that any Institution that proceeds with such retirements will face immediate trade disputes, picketing, and indefinite strike action. For NIMR, this could mean paralysis at a time when Nigeria desperately needs robust medical research to confront public health challenges. The crisis is not just about tenure—it is about the future of research in Nigeria. It is about whether institutions will respect the rules that protect academic careers and ensure continuity in scientific discovery. It is about whether young Nigerians will inherit a research system capable of solving the nation’s health problems. “We have several options,” he said. “We can resume our strike; we can make it a global issue, because that institution has a lot of funding from international agencies.” His language reflects the frustration within the system, but it also highlights the danger of allowing the disagreement to degenerate into a prolonged institutional confrontation. “We will tell the government that he cannot do it. We will take court injunction, we will tell DSS that this man is trying to cause trouble, we can resume our strike, and we can make it a global issue, because that institution has a lot of funding from international agencies. We have several options. He said 31st of August 2026, and if on the 31st, he sees that we have come to occupy NIMR, will he use armoured car to ride over union members, and eject our Research Professors, or will he use AK-47 to kill all of us so that they can eject our research professors, the man wants trouble and he is going to get it.” The view of stakeholders is that NIMR must urgently realign with the law and the clarifications provided by the OHCSF. The premature retirement of Research Directors is not only unlawful but also detrimental to national interest. Nigeria cannot afford to weaken its Research Institutions at a time when global health threats loom large. The laboratories at NIMR must return to their rightful role—pioneering discoveries, mentoring the next generation, and safeguarding the nation’s health. Until then, the crisis remains a sobering reminder of how policy missteps can derail progress, and how the fight for justice in academia is ultimately a fight for the survival of science itself in Nigeria. The post NIMR crisis deepens as research professors face premature retirement appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Balloting underway at 23 polling stations in 2 constituencies of AJK's Bagh district
items.description: Polling is currently underway at 23 stations in two constituencies of Azad Jammu and Kashmir’s Bagh district. Polling began at 8am and will continue till 5pm. In the third phase of polling on Monday, PPP’s Sardar Ziaul Qamar secured 16,637 votes in LA-15 (Bagh Central), followed by PML-N’s Mushtaq Ahmed Minhas with 15,015 and Jamaat-i-Islami’s retired Brig Dr Muhammad Khan with 12,259. But as polling could not be held at nine stations in the constituency, the commission withheld the result. Similarly, the result of LA-16 (Eastern Bagh) was also withheld after polling could not be held at 14 stations, which have a combined 7,238 registered voters. Results from the remaining polling stations showed that PML-N’s Sardar Mir Akbar, who secured 19,515 votes, was leading his closest rival, PPP’s Sardar Qamaruz Zaman, by 3,225 votes. In both constituencies, all five candidates had accused their opponents of massive rigging. “Since we have more than enough police and other law enforcement personnel available, we have made adequate deployment at the polling stations to provide a fear-free environment to voters,” Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) retired Justice Ghulam Mustafa Mughal told Dawn on Saturday. The PML-N bagged 24 seats — nine from Mirpur division in the first phase on July 27 and 15 in the second phase on Aug 2 comprising Muzaffarabad Division and the 12 refugee seats. The PPP, on the other hand, won only 10 constituencies during these phases. The polls are being held in phases amid unrest in the region. The third phase, held on Monday, was originally meant to cover all of Poonch Division, which comprises 11 constituencies, including three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district. However, the AJK Election Commission announced that polling would only go ahead as scheduled in Bagh and Haveli because of concerns over the law and order situation. On Monday, polls went ahead in Bagh and Haveli, but the Election Commission later withheld the results of two constituencies pending repolling at 23 polling stations. It announced the result for LA-14 (Bagh-I), commonly known as Dhirkot, where Jammu Kashmir Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party candidate Sajid Iqbal Abbasi secured a landslide victory with 40,522 votes. LA-17 (Haveli), where AJK Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore was contesting from, emerged as the most contentious constituency. The election was thrown into fresh controversy on Wednesday after the returning officer issued the Form 27 declaring him the winner despite an assurance, according to his PML-N rival Engr Mohsin Aziz, that the result would not be announced until his complaint was taken up by the Election Commission. Aziz subsequently challenged the election, with the AJK Chief Election Co­­mmissioner (CEC) retired Justice Ghulam Mustafa Mughal on Thursday reserving his decision after hearing arguments from both sides.

items.title: I served university for six months, sent away without receiving any salary – Physically-challenged Nwosu
items.description: By Steve Oko For 16 long years after earning his degree from the Abia State University, Uturu, in 2010, Mr. Alexander Nwosu, a Person Living with Disability (PWD), searched for jobs and hopefully held firmly to one belief: that someday he would secure a job and life would smile on him. Despite living with a deformity in one of his legs, Nwosu who hails from Umuda Isingwu, Ohuhu Clan of Umuahia North Local Government Area of Abia State, refused to surrender to despair. Rather than become dependent on charity, he sustained himself by raising and selling seedlings of different plants while searching for meaningful employment. That long-awaited opportunity finally came in 2025 when the Michael Okpara University of Agriculture, Umudike (MOUAU), advertised for vacancies. Like many hopeful applicants, Nwosu applied and was eventually offered employment as an Administrative Assistant Officer in February 2026. For him, it marked the end of years of uncertainty. Filled with excitement, he completed every requirement for the appointment, including medical fitness examinations and other documentations, before resuming duty. He was posted to the Pension Unit, Room 215, in the university’s administrative complex. Every working day, Nwosu climbed the stairs to the second floor despite his physical disability. The daily struggle never discouraged him because he believed the sacrifices would soon be rewarded with his first salary. To sustain himself, he told Vanguard that he even sold some of his personal gadgets to raise transportation fare to work, convinced that once salaries commenced, he would gradually recover from the financial strain. According to him, more than the income, the job represented dignity. It rekindled his hope of becoming financially independent, getting married and raising a family after years of waiting. Sadly that hope has now given way to uncertainty. Months after resuming work, Nwosu said he had yet to receive any salary. Instead, he said that he and several others recently received official letters from the university to stop work and their identity cards were retrieved from them. The development, according to him, followed a meeting where the affected workers were reportedly informed that the institution had been directed to revert to an approved employment quota. According to Nwosu, management explained that although 727 appointments had reportedly been made under the previous administration, the university was given approval to recruit 426 personnel. “The management told us their hands were tied because they had received directives from Abuja to work with the approved number,” Nwosu narrated with tears. Confused by the letter handed to him, Nwosu said he was unsure whether he had been disengaged or was expected to continue reporting for duty. “I don’t even understand what my status is – whether I have been sacked or if I am still a staff member. I am more confused because they have collected my ID card. I have not been paid since I started work. I want clarity and, above all, an opportunity to continue serving,” he said. A copy of the letter titled “RE: OFFER OF APPOINTMENT”, and sighted by our Correspondent read in part: “We refer to earlier correspondence to you on the above subject matter, dated 27th February, 2026 as well as subsequent GIFMIS enrollment exercise undertaken for the enrollment of appointees on the salary platform for the purpose of salary payment. “We regret to inform you that the above mentioned GIFMIS enrollment exercise resulted in your being adjudged “Surplus to Needs”. Therefore, your earlier appointment letter cannot be backed-up with salary payment. It is frustrated until further directives on the subject matter”. Nwosu, however, absolved the current management of the university of any wrongdoing but acknowledged that it had explained its constraints under which it was operating. He, therefore, made a passionate appeal to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the Minister of Education, for their intervention. “I am appealing to Mr President to kindly consider my peculiar situation as a Person With Disability and direct that I be accommodated. I have searched for employment for 16 years after graduation. I don’t want to become a burden to society. I only want to work, earn an honest living and contribute my quota to the nation’s development. “My parents are late. I dream of getting married and raising my own family. Time is running out on me. I am now 45 and I struggled hard to go to university, hoping to have a better life. Returning to the labour market after finally believing I had secured a federal job is emotionally devastating.” Nwosu admitted that the prolonged uncertainty has taken a heavy emotional toll on him. “There are moments when hopeless thoughts come, but I reject them and continue praying that God will touch the hearts of those in authority to intervene. I believe the President is compassionate and will hear our cry.” He added that the situation extends beyond him, noting that several others affected by the development are passing through severe hardship. According to him, the emotional and financial strain has been enormous, with reports that a few of the affected workers, including a pregnant woman, have sadly lost their lives during the period of uncertainty. Meanwhile, a senior university official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the current management should not be blamed for the situation. According to the source, the university is merely implementing directives from the appropriate authorities regarding the approved employment quota. “Whatever is happening is not the making of the current management. Their hands are tied because they are operating within directives from Abuja,” the source explained. Asked whether the affected workers had been dismissed, the official maintained that no formal sack or disengagement had taken place. “We did not sack anybody. We were simply instructed to work with the approved number. If another directive comes from Abuja tomorrow, we will gladly comply. “The Vice-Chancellor is a compassionate leader and would readily accommodate everyone if circumstances permitted. But she is bound by regulations and cannot act outside the directives of the authorities. The letter issued to the affected workers did not use the word ‘sack’.” The University didn’t sack anybody, we’re seeking clarification from Abuja When contacted, the University Registrar, Dr. Nkeiruka Mbanaso, expressed sympathy with the affected workers, insisting, however, that the university did not terminate anybody’s appointment. According to her, the institution is still making efforts to ascertain why some of the newly recruited staff were not captured on the Federal Government’s payroll platform handled by the Office of the Accountant General of the Federation (OAGF). She explained that officials from the Accountant General’s Office conducted the staff capturing exercise at the university and later uploaded the names into the Government Integrated Financial Management Information System (GIFMIS). “After the capturing exercise, the list was forwarded and we confirmed that many of them were captured. However, when the Bursar printed the names that eventually appeared on the GIFMIS platform, we discovered that some persons who had been captured were omitted,” she said. Dr. Mbanaso said the university sought explanations from the visiting officials but was not informed how the final list of beneficiaries was determined. She stressed that the institution had not abandoned the affected workers but had advised those whose names did not appear on the payroll platform to stop reporting for duty pending clarification, noting that it would be unfair for them to continue working without remuneration. “The university did not terminate anybody’s appointment. Capturing for payment is not done by the university but by the Office of the Accountant General in Abuja. We are still making efforts to establish what actually happened and why some staff were not captured for payment,” she added. Ex-Abia SSG urges Tinubu to act swiftly. Meanwhile, an elder statesman and a former Secretary to the Abia State Government (SSG), Dr. Eme Okoro, has appealed passionately to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu to urgently intervene by directing that the affected workers be captured on the Federal Government payroll and allowed to continue with their job. Describing the situation as painful and unfortunate, Dr. Okoro said it was distressing that workers who had faithfully resumed duty and rendered services for months without receiving salaries were now facing uncertainty. “It is heartbreaking, especially at a time when millions of Nigerians are grappling with economic hardship. These young men and women accepted employment in good faith, worked diligently for months and now find themselves in limbo,” he said. The elder statesman urged the President to see the matter as an opportunity to demonstrate compassionate leadership by protecting the hopes and aspirations of the affected workers. He further suggested that the Federal Government could consider expanding MOUAU into a conventional university with broader academic programmes, a move he said would create room for more students, additional staff and greater national development. “Mr President, I respectfully appeal to you to use your good offices to restore hope to these Nigerians. They are not asking for charity; they only seek the opportunity to continue serving their country. Investing in human capital is one of the surest ways to reduce unemployment, discourage crime and strengthen national development. “Please intervene and put smiles back on the faces of these affected workers. They are Nigerians whose only desire is to contribute meaningfully to society through honest employment,” Dr. Okoro pleaded. For Alexander Nwosu, however, the legal and administrative distinctions matter less than the uncertainty surrounding his future. His singular plea is for compassionate intervention. After 16 years of waiting, he says he is not asking for charity, but the opportunity to continue working, earn a living with dignity, marry and raise his own family, and ultimately prove that physical disability should never be a barrier to productivity or hope. Abia Govt urges special consideration for PWDs Special Assistant to the Abia State Governor on Persons Living with Disability, Mr. David Anyaele, urged the federal government to consider PWDs in the recruitment at MOUAU, noting that the Abia State Disability Law prescribes special priority to qualified persons with disabilities in recruitment exercises. He said the law prohibits discrimination in employment and mandates public institutions to reserve opportunities for persons with disabilities, adding that some recruitment procedures are waived in Abia to accommodate their peculiar needs. “The law prohibits discrimination against persons with disabilities in employment. They should be given priority and special consideration during recruitment, with necessary procedures adjusted to reflect their peculiar needs,” Anyaele said. The post I served university for six months, sent away without receiving any salary – Physically-challenged Nwosu appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Jason Arday: 10 things you may not know about British-born Ghanaian former Cambridge professor found dead at 41
items.description: Nearly every major news channel across the globe, alongside social media, is awash with reports on the tragic death of academic Jason Arday, whose life has been cut short. The British-born son of Ghanaian parents who became the youngest Black professor in the history of the University of Cambridge has died at 41. His death came days after he resigned from the university amid allegations concerning plagiarism and questions about aspects of his academic record. He had also just released his memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things . Arday was found unresponsive at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday, August 14. He was pronounced dead at the scene. The Metropolitan Police said the death was unexpected but was not being treated as suspicious, with a file to be prepared for the coroner. His death has since prompted tributes from Cambridge and renewed discussion about his career, the scrutiny he faced and his contribution to debates on race, education and inequality. But who is Jason Arday? Here are 10 things to know about the academic whose life and career have attracted international attention. ——————————————————————————————————————– 1. He was born to Ghanaian parents in London Jason Arday was born and raised in Clapham, south London, to parents who had migrated from Ghana. He grew up as one of four brothers on a council estate. His father, Joseph, worked as a chef, while his mother, Gifty, was a mental health nurse. 2. He was diagnosed with autism at three Arday was diagnosed with autism and global developmental delay when he was three years old. He was non-verbal for much of his childhood and communicated using sign language before he began speaking at about 11. He also had diagnoses including dyslexia and deafness, according to biographical accounts. 3. He did not learn to read and write until he was 18 One of the most notable aspects of Arday’s educational journey was that he only learned to read and write at 18. His early assessments had led some professionals to believe that he would require lifelong support. Instead, he went on to pursue higher education and an academic career. 4. His route into academia was unconventional After gaining his initial qualifications, Arday studied Education Studies and Physical Education before completing further postgraduate studies. He earned a PhD in Education from Liverpool John Moores University. His academic qualifications also included a master’s degree in Education and Pedagogy. 5. He became Cambridge’s youngest Black professor In 2023, at 37, Arday was appointed Professor of Sociology of Education at the University of Cambridge, becoming the youngest Black professor in the university’s history. He had previously held academic positions at the universities of Glasgow and Durham. His research focused particularly on race, inequality, education, mental health and neurodiversity. 6. He had worked outside academia while building his career Arday’s career did not follow a conventional academic path. Before becoming a senior academic, he worked in jobs including at Sainsbury’s and as a cleaner while pursuing his studies and building his academic career. 7. He was an advocate for greater access to higher education Arday used his academic work to campaign for greater representation of Black and minority ethnic people in higher education and for wider access to universities for disadvantaged groups. When his Cambridge appointment was announced, he said his work was focused on opening opportunities for disadvantaged people and helping to “truly democratise higher education”. 8. His academic career came under intense scrutiny in 2026 In the weeks before his death, Arday became the subject of allegations concerning plagiarism in some of his academic work. Reports examined passages in his 2015 doctoral thesis and other publications. Arday denied deliberately plagiarising material but acknowledged what he described as previous scholarly “mistakes”. The University of Cambridge subsequently announced an investigation after receiving new information concerning his academic qualifications and honorary appointments. 9. He resigned from Cambridge shortly before his death Arday announced on August 5 that he was leaving his Cambridge position and his fellowship at Jesus College with immediate effect. In his resignation statement, he said the controversy and public scrutiny had taken a profound toll on him and those close to him. His departure came less than two weeks before his death. 10. He had just published a memoir Arday’s memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things , was released in the United States on August 11, 2026, just three days before his death. The book recounts aspects of his upbringing, education and rise through academia, making its release particularly significant given the events surrounding the final days of his life.

items.title: KNUST partners with government to manufacture locally-made agricultural machines and smart traffic lights
items.description: The Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology is set to partner with the Ministry of Food and Agriculture to develop locally produced farming equipment and technologies aimed at reducing Ghana’s dependence on imports. Vice-Chancellor of KNUST, Professor Christian Agyare, gave the assurance when he received the Deputy Minister for Food and Agriculture and MP for Ayawaso West Wuogon, Hon. John Dumelo, at his office. Mr Dumelo said the Ministry undertakes significant procurement annually and believes more of such contracts should go to solutions developed by Ghanaian universities. “We should be able to change the norm to allow most of our university students to come up with designs that we can expand on to reduce importation,” he said. He added that the long-term objective is to increase the use of locally developed technologies in government projects, particularly in agriculture where equipment and mechanisation remain a major challenge. The Deputy Minister further proposed that KNUST’s engineering departments lead the design and manufacturing of agricultural machines and tools that can be deployed to farmers nationwide. Responding, Professor Agyare described the proposal as “a laudable initiative” that aligns with his vision of positioning KNUST at the centre of national development. “This aligns with the University’s strategic vision of strengthening partnerships that enable KNUST to translate its expertise and research into practical solutions,” he said. He urged relevant departments to engage Mr Dumelo to explore areas of mutual interest in agricultural mechanisation. The MP explored partnerships on Smart traffic lights, manufactured by KNUST. Beyond agriculture, the meeting also explored a second collaboration,that is,the development of locally manufactured traffic-light systems for Hon. Dumelo’s Ayawaso West Wuogon constituency. Leading the KNUST delegation, Professor Eric Tutu Tchao, Scientific Director of the DIPPER Lab in the College of Engineering, said discussions at the Lab had focused on a proposed project to improve traffic-light systems in the constituency. According to Prof. Tchao, the project will require collaboration between the College of Engineering and the College of Science, with university experts providing technical support to address traffic challenges. Mr Dumelo recalled that as a student at KNUST, traffic lights had previously been developed by students, and he expressed interest in reviving that model. “We would like to explore the possibility of engaging KNUST students and faculty to design and manufacture systems that could be deployed within the constituency,” he said. He noted that beyond Ayawaso West Wuogon, the initiative could provide a model for replication across the country. The Vice-Chancellor assured the Deputy Minister of KNUST’s full support and technical capacity to deliver on both projects. The DIPPER Lab will lead the technical implementation of the traffic-light project, in collaboration with experts from the College of Engineering and the College of Science.

items.title: Ex-Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism scandal found dead
items.description: Black academic Jason Arday, who resigned from the University of Cambridge last week following a high-profile plagiarism scandal that raised claims of racism, was found dead on Friday, the prestigious British institution confirmed. Arday, 41, was found unresponsive Friday afternoon at an address in south London, according to the capital’s Metropolitan Police Service, which did not confirm the identity of the deceased person at the time of discovery. “We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news,” Cambridge University’s top administrator, Vice Chancellor Deborah Prentice, said in a brief statement. Arday’s family criticised what they called a “campaign of harassment” that followed allegations about his academic work and personal life. “The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone,” the family said in a statement released through his publisher Simon & Schuster. The scandal erupted after some academics and media reports accused Arday, who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, of plagiarising parts of his doctoral thesis. The allegations have been seized on by British right-wing newspapers and commentators, who claim that he unfairly benefited from diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies. Arday announced on August 5 that he was resigning from both his university post as a professor and as a fellow of Jesus College, shortly after they announced probes into the various accusations. In a letter posted online, Arday said that quitting was “the only way” to end a “difficult period”, but insisted the decision should not be “mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me”. Newspaper claims Police said officers had been called by the London Ambulance Service “following a report that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property” in the city’s Battersea neighbourhood. “Sadly, a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene,” it said in a statement, noting his next-of-kin had been informed. “At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. “The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s Central South Command Unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner.” Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was “deeply shocked (and) saddened” by the news. She urged people to give his family “privacy through this incredibly difficult period (and) to remember there are real people with loved ones involved”. The furore around Arday grew after Nathan Cofnas, a US academic and self-defined “race realist” — whose Cambridge research affiliation ended in 2024 amid racism accusations — published claims about him in July. The allegations included that multiple sections of Arday’s doctoral dissertation were copied from other works. The Times and Telegraph newspapers have published several investigative articles into Arday’s academic work and personal life. Some of his claims about his personal life, including that he once ran 30 marathons in 35 days and raised millions for charities, were also disputed. ‘Racially motivated’ In an interview with The Times earlier this month, Arday admitted making academic “mistakes” but said he was being wrongly “portrayed to be a liar and a fantasist and an academic fraud”. He also alleged the “campaign to unseat me from my position” was “racially motivated”. The controversy around Arday appears to have divided the Cambridge campus and wider academia. A group of university academics last week wrote to Prentice slamming Arday’s appointment and asking her to appoint an independent body to probe what happened. Others have written joint letters in support of him. On Wednesday, Prentice had called his alleged wrongdoing “an aberration” and vowed a thorough and transparent investigation, while insisting it should not be used “to cast aspersions” on other academics from ethnic minority backgrounds. The American psychologist promised the probe would look into the “circumstances” of Arday’s appointment and his time in post that would include academics from “beyond Cambridge”. Arday’s memoir — Great and Unfortunate Things — had been published in the United States the previous day, ahead of its planned release in Britain later this month. It has also attracted scrutiny.

Deployment tearing military homes apart: Experts propose 12-point rescue plan
items.description: By Nkiruka Nnorom & Matthew Johnson Experts at the 2nd National Military Fathers’ Leadership Summit have warned that repeated deployments and prolonged absence of military men, who are fathers, are weakening homes in barracks across Nigeria, with direct consequences for children’s education, discipline and emotional well-being. Held in Lagos on Thursday with the theme: “Military Fathers as Protectors: Strengthening Families, Securing Communities”, the summit brought together serving officers, spouses, educators and civil society groups to address what speakers described as a silent crisis in military households. They need support, not just medals Speaking, Founder\CEO, SheSafety and Health Initiative, Ambassador Mabel Abel-Onaiwu, called for greater attention to the emotional wellbeing, safety and emergency preparedness of men in the Armed Forces. Onaiwu, who served in the military for over 12 years, said her experience exposed significant gaps in support systems for personnel and their families. “Safety and security go hand in hand. Personnel are often expected to respond to emergencies, including fires, accidents and disasters, regardless of whether they have received adequate emergency-response training,” she said. She noted that SheSafety had in the last two years trained more than 2,000 women in three major military barracks and police formations in Lagos as part of empowerment and safety projects. The former soldier urged Nigerians to recognise serving personnel as living heroes whose sacrifices must be appreciated while they are alive. “We don’t believe in be a man and then you slump and die. The worst thing that can happen to you is for you to drop dead because when you do, life continues, and we don’t want that for the men,” she said. “The summit is an annual national event dedicated to celebrating and supporting men in the Armed Forces. We don’t want just the Armed Forces Remembrance Day, where the fallen heroes have been given flowers. We want these living heroes to also receive their flowers while they are here.” Strength of the Army depends on families behind them Lieutenant MJ Abdul-Kareem, who represented the Commander, 9 Brigade, Nigerian Army, Brig.-Gen. A.O. Owolabi, said military men, who are fathers face unique challenges because their duties often keep them away from home for long periods. “Providing for a child is important, but being available to listen, advise, encourage and guide the child is equally important. The Nigerian Army depends not only on the physical strength of its personnel, but also the strength, stability and support of the families behind them,” he said. He urged fathers to focus on the legacy of values they leave for their children, stressing that ranks and appointments will fade but discipline and character endure. 12-point plan to rescue military families Guest speaker and Dean, Faculty of Education, University of Lagos, Prof. Simeon Adebayo Oladipo, said Nigeria’s security and the well-being of military families are interdependent, not competing goals. He argued that a father who is well-supported at home is better positioned to protect the nation abroad, and that neglecting military children’s education and emotional welfare weakens national security infrastructure. “The role of a military father involves a double burden of protecting the nation in uniform and protecting the household at home. And the second role is harder to see and rarely funded,” he said. Citing Nigeria’s projected population of 242 million in 2026, Prof. Oladipo said any weakness in child upbringing is “multiplied across tens of millions of households before it is felt at the level of the nation.” He said evidence from military communities shows deployment often leads to loneliness, poor supervision, disruptive schooling and, in some cases, rise in problematic behaviour among children, especially boys. “When the father is deployed, our mothers begin to look here and there for the safety of the fathers. You never can tell whether they will go or return. That’s why it is a risk to the family. They surrender their lives for the security of the nation. We need to acknowledge it. It is our duty,” he said. The professor added that frequent postings and relocations compound the problem, as children in military households often change schools, teachers and peer groups multiple times, affecting academic performance. He, however, noted that most current support focuses on physical infrastructure, health and general welfare, with less attention to communication between schools and deployed fathers, and to counseling for children. To bridge the gap, Prof. Oladipo proposed a 12-point rescue plan. He said that dedicated school-family communication structures should be established to enable deployed fathers to receive academic reports and send recorded messages to their children. He also said that counseling and mentorship support systems should be built into military schools as a standing service, with special attention to adolescent boys and girls. “There should be predictability in postings in terms of frequency, notice and duration so that spouses and schools can plan ahead. A continuity protocol for military dependents should be introduced, including standardized transfer of academic records and priority placement in new schools. Guaranteed communication access for deployed fathers should be treated as part of operational logistics, even in areas with poor connectivity,” he advised. Prof. Oladipo said the remaining recommendations in the 12-point plan address data tracking, policy reforms and partnerships to ensure military children feel the benefits of their fathers’ service. The first edition of the summit focused on the Nigerian Navy and provided a platform for personnel to openly discuss challenges affecting them and their families, organisers said. The post Deployment tearing military homes apart: Experts propose 12-point rescue plan appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Nigerian football: Westerhof writes President Tinubu
items.description: Nigerian football has seen better days. Unfortunately, those days – when an everyday football fan on the street could name Nigeria’s first X1 offhandedly – have become a very distant past. After the heroics of the 1980 AFCON winning era, Nigerian football blossomed again between 1990 – ‘98. That was a period Nigerians rightly call the golden era of modern Nigerian football folklore. The architect of that memorable spell, Clemens Westerhof is still very much attached to Nigeria, long after leaving the Super Eagles at the expiration of his contract in 1994. He was engaged in 1989 as coach of the national team. Westerhof took the Super Eagles to win silver medal in his maiden AFCON appearance in 1990. They won bronze at Senegal 1992 after defeating Cameroon 2-1 in the third-place playoff match with goals from Friday Ekpo and Rashidi Yekini. In 1994 he put the icing on the cake by winning the AFCON in Tunisia and qualified Nigeria to her first FIFA World Cup finals. At the tournament in the USA, Nigeria played so well that the Super Eagles were rated joint most entertaining side in the world with Brazil and ranked 5th best national team by FIFA, the highest by an African team. The then military Head of State General Sani Abacha promised a house to reward each of the squad members and officials, but only a handful received theirs instantly. Coach Clemens Westerhof eventually got his house 30 years after, during the reign of late President Mohammadu Buhari. “It’s taken a long go-slow, but I feel happy that my second country has fulfilled its promise to me,” said Westerhof after receiving keys to the house from the then Minister of Works Babatunde Raji Fashola. “I always say Nigeria gave me everything as a man and in football. You can see that I wasn’t wrong. I thank everyone involved in making this happen,” an appreciative Westerhof reflected. However, there is an uncomfortable twist to the story. Westerhof is not at ease with the location of the house. With the scale of insecurity in the country, the Dutchman is pleading with President Bola Ahmed Tinubu to consider a fresh allocation of a property in a more secure environment where he and his family can sleep with both eyes closed, without fear any time he visits on holiday. In an open letter to the President, Westerhof pleads, “The house is located in a remote area of Gwagwalada, near Kuje, within the Federal Capital Territory. It’s in a remote part of FCT. And because of the prevailing security concerns, including the risk of kidnapping, we have been strongly advised that it is unsafe for us to live there or even visit whenever we travel to Nigeria.” The house is a four bedroom bungalow. On a recent visit to Nigeria, the former Super Eagles coach was promised by the then minister of housing, Ahmed Musa Dangiwa that the reallocation would be in not more than a year. Chairman of the Sports Commission , Shehu Diko facilitated Dangiwa’s meeting with Westerhof. “For all you did for Nigeria, the reallocation you’re asking for would be done with all pleasure,” Dangiwa told Westerhof in his office. “In a few months, that will be done,” the minister assured, even asking Westerhof if he wanted another bungalow or an apartment in a better area. However, with the change of the minister the case appears forgotten,” prompting Westerhof’s letter to President Tinubu. The coach is worried that his desire to visit, and perhaps spend quality time in the country with his family is being impeded by the slow response from government thus the open appeal. “Nigeria has given me memories that I will cherish forever. The affection of the Nigerian people has never faded, neither has my affection for Nigeria,” he said. The coach continued, “I remain proud to have worn the green and white with honour. I remain proud of every player, every supporter, and every Nigerian who believed in us.” In conclusion he wrote, “Your Excellency, I humbly ask for your kind intervention so that this matter may be resolved. It would mean more to my family than words can express, and it would reaffirm the enduring bond between Nigeria and one of its grateful former coaches.” The post Nigerian football: Westerhof writes President Tinubu appeared first on Vanguard News .

Delta’s Izeze: From commissioner’s office to custody
items.description: By Jimitota Onoyume, Assistant News Editor For a politician who only recently moved between the corridors of power and the construction sites of Delta State, the present reality for Commissioner for Works, Reuben Izeze, is a dramatic change of scene. The commissioner Izeze, as his fondly called, has been suspended by the Delta State Government and subsequently remanded at the Warri correction centre following his arraignment in connection with the violent incident involving Governor Sheriff Oborevwori’s protocol aide, Simon Mudi, aka Temple . The legal process unfolds. But beyond the courtroom and the walls of the custodial centre lies a bigger question: what exactly happened at the Petroleum Training Institute (PTI), and what was behind the violent confrontation that has now assumed this dimension? The incident occurred during a Delta Central All Progressives Congress stakeholders’ meeting at the PTI. The gathering, which brought together prominent political figures from the senatorial district, was reportedly convened as part of preparations for future elections. The political meeting itself, however, was described by the governor’s Executive Assistant on Politics, Jennifer Adasen, as peaceful and successful. In a statement issued after videos of the violence emerged, she said the meeting was “peaceful, well-organised and concluded successfully in an atmosphere of unity, mutual respect and constructive engagement.” She condemned the violence, stressing that the altercation occurred outside the venue of the meeting. That distinction is important because the violence has since overshadowed the original purpose of the political gathering. At the centre of the controversy is Mudi, aka Temple, who has spoken publicly about his experience. According to accounts attributed to him in the media, Mudi said he was on his way to eat when he was alerted that a group of people had arrived and that there might be an attack. He alleged that several men descended on him, breaking bottles and stabbing him multiple times. “On that day, he came again with over 50 boys. In fact, what really happened was that I was on my way to eat with my watchmen. When my associate called me that he saw a signal they had brought a lot of boys to attack me, immediately I dropped the call and saw about 12 boys who came to attack me. “Before I could say anything, they started breaking bottles everywhere, stabbing me from the back, stabbing me everywhere. Everyone was running. I couldn’t even defend myself “, he recalled. He said he had done eleven stitches so far. He also alleged that the incident was not an isolated occurrence, claiming that he had earlier been attacked during a burial ceremony at Okwagbe in Ughelli South Local Government Area. According to him , a commissioner was behind the attacks, an allegation that has not been established by a court. “But before this latest incident he had attacked me on the 26th of last month during our late brother’s burial in Okwagbe with over 24 boys. “I don’t know how a commissioner can set up another commissioner. There must be justice. How can over 70 boys attack one person? It was a terrible thing to do. I have had eleven stitches “, Mudi alleged. The allegation has inevitably fuelled speculation that the violence could have roots in a political or personal disagreement involving influential actors within the state’s political structure. But speculation is not proof. And this is where the ongoing investigation and court proceedings become particularly significant. Governor Oborevwori has said the decision to suspend Izeze was to allow the police to investigate the matter without interference. The state government has also publicly condemned the violence and directed security agencies to identify and prosecute those found responsible. The suspension and subsequent court proceedings have therefore transformed what initially appeared to be another episode of political violence into a matter attracting considerable public attention. For Izeze, the immediate challenge is to deal with the legal process and the allegations surrounding the incident. For the government, it is a test of its commitment to accountability, especially when those involved are politically exposed persons. For the public, perhaps the most important expectation is simple: that the truth should emerge. While the legal battle continues, reports have also emerged about Izeze’s conduct at the Warri Correctional Centre. An unconfirmed report circulating in recent days claimed that the suspended commissioner has been relating cordially with other inmates and has allegedly paid fines for some inmates who were unable to meet their financial obligations. The same report claimed that he was considering organising a football competition for inmates, with the proposed theme “Ukodo na Tevwe – the pottage has reached inmates ”, centred on Governor Oborevwori’s popular Ukodo ( pottage ) political slogan. There were also claims that Izeze was exploring a possible collaboration with the Niger Delta Development Commission on a water project for the correctional facility. These reports if eventually confirmed, they would add another dimension to the story of a commissioner whose public profile has suddenly shifted from road construction and government projects to legal proceedings and custodial life. Doing good in custody counts for inmates. Life can be funny sometimes .Izeze was still actively speaking about major road projects in Delta only weeks before the controversy. In July, for instance, he discussed the state government’s intervention on the Warri-Benin Highway and other infrastructure projects. Today, his political and administrative future is temporarily overshadowed by a case now before the court. And he is currently occupying a space at the Warri correction centre as his temporary abode. Will the case be decided in a matter of days ,weeks ? Will Izeze return to his post as a Commissioner in the administration of governor Oborevwori? Time will tell. The post Delta’s Izeze: From commissioner’s office to custody appeared first on Vanguard News .
