items.title: A Bleak, Violent Novel’s Unexpected Delights
items.description: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. Before his latest book, Marlon James hadn’t written a novel set in Jamaica in more than a decade. In the years following his Booker Prize–winning A Brief History of Seven Killings , the author focused on his Dark Star Trilogy , set in a fantasy universe. But after that long literary detour, he returned to the land of his birth in his new novel, The Disappearers —which is set primarily in Kingston and follows a group of characters, all queer Jamaican men, who meet while rehearsing a play that will never be seen. First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: Hard-luck men in hardscrabble towns “Disunion,” a short story by Kurt Andersen A deeply layered novel about masculinity “Stance,” a poem by Deborah Garrison For this group, which gathers in secret in 1988, seeing and being seen are matters of life and death. The Kingston they inhabit is murderously homophobic, and accordingly, the novel can be quite bleak. But The Disappearers offers some delights too. Recently, in her article about the book for The Atlantic , Stephanie Burt noted that “the novel opens up many pleasures for literary readers,” who may recognize the numerous titles and references sprinkled throughout. I was deeply affected by how, almost universally, the characters seek out anything that proves that gay life exists on a larger scale. Lowbrow works, such as porn films and magazines, are most accessible; Playgirl and Hustler are name-checked. The songs of Boy George, Sylvester, and Prince are lifelines—the homoerotic cover of Prince’s 1988 album, Lovesexy , is an especially powerful beacon. Many of the characters are well read, and they name-drop gay novels such as Andrew Holleran’s Dancer From the Dance and E. M. Forster’s Maurice . For one of the men in particular, the type of hustling, defiant gay life that John Rechy describes in his nonfiction book The Sexual Outlaw is pivotal. The play they put on, a 1967 drama called Fortune and Men’s Eyes , explores homosexuality among a group of prisoners. Some of its characters see sex as a means for gaining or establishing power; others, as a convenient way to access pleasure. Some are what a modern audience might recognize as gay, whereas others choose partners largely because of their proximity. The cast share the characters’ disparate attitudes toward queerness. But in the Jamaica they live in, there is no room for nuance; any man seen as homosexual is a target for violence. Brutality will soon come to the rehearsal room. In a way, James has written a gay novel about the uses of a gay novel. When his characters invoke Oscar Wilde and Edmund White, Hadrian and Michelangelo, they’re proving, to themselves and to the reader, that queer life existed long before they came around. But James is not an unskeptical cheerleader for the healing power of visibility and representation. The Disappearers ’ major theme, after all, is that being recognized can be a bad thing: Owning these books is a hazard. Buying Lovesexy as a man in 1988 Kingston invites vigilantism. Staging Fortune and Men’s Eyes puts its cast and crew in danger. So why try to do it? The director and ringleader, Havelock Titus, asks himself this question more than a decade after those hopeful rehearsals. He knew, even at the time, that the effort was a risk. He still doesn’t know “what success would have meant,” because the unstaged play “never had the chance to become a failure.” But Havelock knows on some level that he did it because, just like those who came before him, he wanted to create some kind of evidence that gay men communed and survived in his time and place. In short, he was tired of being erased. Illustration by Roche Marlon James Returns to Realism, and to Jamaica By Stephanie Burt In his new novel, gay men struggle to escape violence in Kingston. Read the full article. What to Read The Age of Reform , by Richard Hofstadter History can’t fully explain the present or predict the future, but it can help us understand the patterns of contemporary politics and the likely paths ahead. In 1955, Hofstadter, one of the great American historians of the 20th century, published The Age of Reform —a political and social history of the years 1890 to 1940, the period of populism, progressivism, and the New Deal. Rapid technological change, monopoly power, deep inequality, endemic corruption, mass immigration, nativist demagogues, the transformation of both political parties, repeated efforts at reform, recurring spasms of reaction: Perhaps no other age so resembles our own. Hofstadter is brilliant at analyzing types that feel quite familiar to us today—the crusading urban progressive, the small-town conspiracy theorist. He was a liberal who sympathized with the passion for progress while unsentimentally diagnosing its illiberal ideas and motives. The fevered moralism of that age seems a long way from the paralyzing cynicism of ours. But reading Hofstadter will remind you that reform and reaction not only follow each other, but also often coexist in the same moment; neither ever has the last word. Americans are always dreaming of a better country, and some have actually made it so. — George Packer From our list: What’s the one book that explains American politics today? Out Next Week 📚 Finding Renée Richards , by Julie Kliegman 📚 The Jackal: The Rise and Fall of Carlos, the World’s First Super-Terrorist , by Joby Warrick 📚 The Book of Chuck , by LaToya Watkins Your Weekend Read Illustration by Ben Hickey Bring Back the Blue-Book Exam By Walt Hunter Universities find themselves in a surprising position. The only reliable way to evaluate what students have learned may be to bring back pen and paper. Faculty are reverting to in-person, handwritten assignments and timed essays—anything that keeps assessments offline. The unlikely hero of the day is the blue book, sales of which are up by as much as 80 percent for some universities since 2023. Read the full article. items.title: Sudan Nashra: In cross-border offensive, RSF seizes Blue Nile’s Geisan, recaptures Kurmuk | Military repels major RSF attack on North Kordofan’s Gabra al-Sheikh | After clashes inside Kauda, SPLM-N-Otoro fighting spreads to nearby villages | Kordofan governor in RSF-led govt defects | Back-to-back Sudanese visits to Juba in mutual push to contain border, Abyei tensions
items.description: Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . The Rapid Support Forces and its allies launched a broad offensive across Sudan this week, opening simultaneous attacks on multiple fronts in what military officers described to Mada Masr as an attempt to offset heavy losses on the North Kordofan front and prevent military advances westward. From an attempt to retake a strategic border area in Darfur to waves of drone strikes across northern and central Sudan that kept the military’s air defenses heavily engaged, the escalation culminated with major gains in Blue Nile. The RSF and its ally the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, seized Geisan on Tuesday and retook Kurmuk two days later, advancing from SPLM-N-held territory in southern Blue Nile and across the Ethiopian border, three military sources told Mada Masr. The gains reverse much of the military’s recent progress along the southeastern border, coming only weeks after it recaptured Kurmuk and disrupted the cross-border supply routes that had sustained the allies’ campaign in the region. As the two sides were fighting in Kurmuk, an RSF force of more than 250 combat vehicles moved on Gabra al-Sheikh, one of the paramilitary group’s main logistics hub in North Kordofan, in an attempt to retake the area it lost in the military’s late-July offensive. The military and allied forces repelled the attack after several hours of fighting. While the SPLM-N remains occupied on the Blue Nile front, an internal crisis is growing in its South Kordofan stronghold, a crisis that could, a former military source in the movement said, force it to divert forces and resources to protecting its own territory from its own people. Clashes that broke out last week in Kauda, the movement’s seat of power, between SPLM-N forces and one of its oldest constituencies, the Otoro tribe, were brought under control within days. But this week, the confrontation spread to villages surrounding the town, where clashes and heavy artillery exchanges have driven a new wave of displacement. SPLM-N has since deployed heavily around Kauda to prevent the fighting from reaching the town again, a buildup that has disrupted people’s daily lives and deepened the strain on communities already exhausted by months of intermittent clashes and tightening security measures, three residents told Mada Masr. At the root of the latest violence are Otoro demands for greater representation in the movement’s civilian and military institutions — a pushback against what they see as an increasingly centralized mode of governance. Tribal notables in SPLM-N territory warn that without genuine outreach to local communities, the violence will keep recurring, testing the movement’s claim to offer a model of local governance distinct from central state rule and risking a deeper rift between its institutions and the people they govern. The RSF-led government is facing its own internal fractures. A fourth high-profile defection hit the administrative structures it has built in western Sudan, with Hamad Khalifa, the governor of the Kordofan region in the RSF-led Tasis administration and a member of its presidential council, announcing Wednesday that he is exiting the group. In the military-led government, Khartoum is accelerating its push for a domestic political track, targeting September for the launch of the intra-Sudanese dialogue Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has spent months championing and preparing — a process he wants to use to rebuild state institutions and set the terms for the next phase of the country’s political order under state oversight. The push picked up pace after international mediation in Addis Ababa broke down in late July, giving the government an opening to move ahead with its own track inside the country, a political source informed of the process said. The government is now working to settle the dialogue’s preparatory arrangements, from the composition of the committee that will organize it to the rules for participation and the issues to be addressed first. But those arrangements are themselves a source of contention, with the opposition Sumud coalition arguing that the forces expected to take part should have a say in shaping them, given that they will effectively determine the course of the process and its outcomes. Khartoum is also working with Juba through security talks to build direct channels between the two countries’ military and security agencies, as both sides seek to contain tensions along their shared border, Sudanese and South Sudanese sources told Mada Masr. A month of high-level contacts between the two capitals continued this week with back-to-back visits to Juba by Sudan’s Defense Minister Hassan Kabron and Darfur Governor Minni Arko Minnawi. Talks focused on preventing armed groups and military supplies from crossing the border, protecting oil infrastructure crucial to both economies and managing tensions around the disputed Abyei area, after South Sudan decided to include it as an electoral district in its first general elections scheduled in December. *** In cross-border offensive, RSF seizes Blue Nile’s Geisan, recaptures Kurmuk RSF fighters and their allies, the SPLM-N (Hilu) forces led by Joseph Toka, attack the town of Geisan in Blue Nile state, August 11. Courtesy: Sudan War Monitor The RSF and its ally the SPLM-N have rapidly reversed the military’s recent gains in southeastern Blue Nile, seizing Geisan on Tuesday and retaking Kurmuk days later in an offensive launched from SPLM-N-held territory and across the Ethiopian border, three military sources told Mada Masr. The offensive has brought the two sides back into a fight over the state’s most strategically important border positions, only weeks after the military recaptured Kurmuk. The key cross-border gateway had fallen to the RSF and SPLM-N in March after the allies moved into Blue Nile from Ethiopia, opening a route for supplies and military support to reach their forces. The military’s July advance had put it on course to regain control of the southeastern border and disrupt the supply routes that had sustained its rivals’ campaign. Geisan appears to have then emerged as a major objective for the RSF and its allies. Its location near the Ethiopian border makes it strategically important as an alternative corridor for movement and supplies. The RSF-SPLM-N alliance began mobilizing for an offensive on Geisan shortly after losing Kurmuk in July. For a former military officer, the offensive in Blue Nile is a bid by the RSF to secure a compensatory victory after its heavy defeats on the Kordofan front and the military’s takeover of the Khartoum-Kordofan Saderat Road. According to the former officer, the group is also seeking to open a new front along the border that could stretch the military’s forces and disrupt its plans to expand westward toward Darfur. The offensive was prepared from across the border, according to the military sources. After withdrawing from Kurmuk in July , the RSF regrouped at camps in Asosa, in Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region, which borders Sudan, a military source said. The fighters were reinforced with additional personnel, including mercenaries of various nationalities who had undergone advanced military training in recent weeks ahead of the assault on Geisan, the source added. RSF fighters and their allies attacked Geisan in the early hours of Tuesday from two main axes, from the south and east, a second military source told Mada Masr. The assault was launched from inside Ethiopian territory and was accompanied by heavy drone strikes targeting military defenses and several key sites in the town, the source said. By Tuesday evening, the RSF had fully taken control of Geisan, after the military withdrew to Bakori, about 20 km from Damazin, where it maintains a large garrison, the source said. New troops have since arrived from Damazin to reinforce the area and reorganize ahead of a counteroffensive to retake Geisan, they added. The RSF-led Tasis alliance announced on the same day that it secured control of Geisan and inflicted heavy losses on the military in personnel and equipment. In a statement, the alliance said it seized all military positions in the town, along with large quantities of weapons and military equipment. Geisan’s importance stems not only from its location on the Ethiopian border, but also its wider strategic position in Blue Nile State. The town lies about 75 km southeast of the state capital Damazin and around 65 km from Roseires Dam, which supplies electricity to large parts of Sudan and provides irrigation for major agricultural schemes. From Geisan, the offensive then turned toward Kurmuk. Over the following days, strategic and suicide drones, along with heavy artillery fire launched from Ethiopian territory, pummeled Kurmuk, according to a third military source and a statement from the Kurmuk administration. On Thursday, the RSF and its allies moved on Kurmuk, attacking from three directions: from their new positions in Geisan to the northeast, from Ethiopian territory to the east and from the south, through areas controlled by the SPLM-N faction led by Joseph Toka, the military source said. The military withdrew toward Sali, north of Kurmuk, while its air force continued striking RSF positions inside the town, the source said. A local administrator in Asosa told Mada Masr that heavy infantry units were observed moving from an RSF base inside Ethiopia toward the border with Blue Nile state prior to Thursday’s attack. The official said he saw waves of military vehicles mounted with artillery moving toward the border, as well as soldiers wearing RSF uniforms. More than 20 civilians were killed in Geisan’s clashes on Tuesday, according to the UN. The International Organization for Migration said it recorded the displacement of around 2,500 people from Geisan to other locations within the locality. Others crossed into Ethiopia. The Geisan locality administration described the RSF attack as a “fully fledged crime” targeting residents’ livelihoods and security, particularly as they were busy cultivating their land for the agricultural season critical for food security. The third military source suggested that the RSF forces and its ally are unlikely to advance much farther, given the difficult terrain and the onset of heavy rains, which severely restrict the movement of personnel and vehicles. The military is expected to rely primarily on aerial attacks to wear down the RSF before launching any ground operation to retake Kurmuk, the source added. The former officer warned that Addis Ababa’s continued hosting of RSF training camps and launch points used to stage operations inside Sudan carries a regional risk under current circumstances — with Sudanese-Ethiopian relations already strained, and Ethiopia itself facing renewed instability in Tigray. Fighting broke out in early August between federal forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front in Western Tigray, which borders Sudan. If Khartoum responded in kind to Ethiopian support for the RSF, the former officer said, the confrontation could trigger a broader regional crisis. *** RSF launches simultaneous drone attacks on four cities The RSF launched a wave of suicide drone attacks on four cities in northern and central Sudan on Wednesday morning. Military ground defenses intercepted some of the drones before they reached their intended targets, according to three eyewitnesses who spoke to Mada Masr. In River Nile State, more than 20 RSF suicide drones targeting the cities of Damer and Atbara were shot down by military air defenses around the time of the dawn call to prayer, an eyewitness told Mada Masr. Explosions were heard until 6 am, the witness said. In Khartoum, an eyewitness in Bahri said RSF drones targeted civilian and military sites in northern and western Omdurman, as well as several locations in Bahri’s Doroshab area, including a mosque and a power station. Some of the drones were intercepted by air defenses, the witness said, and there were no casualties. In North Kordofan’s Obeid, several drones targeted the city, with one striking an area near a grocery store and a bank, killing a woman who had gone to the bank to collect her monthly pension and an employee of the judicial authority, an eyewitness said. The strikes led authorities to suspend work at several public facilities, close several schools and shut down Obeid’s main market. RSF drones returned to Omdurman on Thursday, an official in the city told Mada Masr, but no casualties were reported. *** New RSF attack on West Darfur’s Bir Saliba repelled The military-allied joint force repels an RSF attack on Bir Saliba in West Darfur, August 8. Courtesy: @AbedaMoham6183 on X The RSF launched a new attack on Bir Saliba in West Darfur on Saturday but was repelled by the military-allied joint force of armed movements, the latest in a series of attempts to regain control of the strategic border area with Chad. The joint force stated that the attack began in the early morning along two axes, from Kulbus to the northwest and Sileia to the north. It said its forces destroyed more than 38 combat vehicles, captured another 27 with their equipment and killed the commander of the attacking force along with several other fighters. A military source told Mada Masr that the attackers advanced in large numbers, prompting the joint force to repeat the tactic it had used in previous battles: withdrawing before encircling the advancing force and launching a counterattack. The RSF is now mobilizing fighters in Kulbus, Sileia and Sirba in preparation for another attack on Bir Saliba, the source said. Bir Saliba, about 30 km north of West Darfur capital Geneina, sits on the Sudan-Chad border and serves as a key supply corridor. Control of the area allows forces to monitor cross-border movement, prevent infiltration and flanking maneuvers and secure routes leading north toward Gargira and Tina in North Darfur, where the military maintains major operational bases. The area has changed hands several times since the war began. The military recaptured it on July 11 during a campaign that brought military and allied forces within reach of Geneina. *** Joint force briefly pushes into North Darfur’s Ambro before RSF restores control The joint force of military-allied armed movements launched a surprise attack on RSF positions in the border town of Ambro, North Darfur, on Thursday. A field source in the joint force told Mada Masr their forces captured several combat vehicles before withdrawing from the area later that day. An RSF source, however, said the group had drawn the attackers into an ambush, destroying and capturing several vehicles and killing the commander of the attacking force. The RSF captured Ambro, along the Chadian border, on June 23 as part of an offensive that brought the group deeper into the Zaghawa tribal territory, where the military retains its last positions in Darfur following the fall of Fasher last year. At the time, the RSF fighters launching the assault looted and burned homes, killing and injuring civilians and forcing large numbers of families to flee. *** Military repels major RSF attack on North Kordofan’s Gabra al-Sheikh The RSF launched a large-scale assault on North Kordofan’s Gabra al-Sheikh on Thursday, seeking to retake one of its main logistics hubs in the state weeks after losing it to the military. The military and allied forces repelled the attack after several hours of fighting, according to a military statement and two military sources who spoke to Mada Masr. Gabra al-Sheikh fell to the military in late July as part of a two-day surprise offensive that secured five towns within a 300-square-kilometer area and restored military control over the Saderat Road cutting across North Kordofan. The RSF had used the area to move reinforcements from Darfur via the road and a web of dirt tracks that allowed it to maneuver and redeploy in the region with relative ease. The RSF attacked Gabra al-Sheikh on Thursday with more than 250 combat vehicles, military spokesperson Assem Awad said in a press statement. The military repelled the assault and inflicted heavy losses in personnel and equipment, forcing the attacking forces to withdraw toward Darfur, he said. A member of the Dar Hamar emergency room in West Kordofan told Mada Masr that the RSF had spent the days prior preparing for offensives on Bara and Gabra al-Sheikh. According to a military source, the paramilitary group had amassed forces in the Wudyan, Abu Hadid and Um Surra areas near Gabra al-Sheikh, using the areas’ vegetation as cover to conceal its movements from military aircraft. On Thursday, the fighters moved on the town from three directions and fighting lasted for several hours, involving heavy and light weapons, alongside extensive drone activity, according to a field source affiliated with the military. The attacking force included advanced combat vehicles and weapons, as well as mercenaries of several nationalities, including Libyans and Colombians, the source said. The military captured around 65 combat vehicles and destroyed more than 80 others, the source added. Mohamed Didan, the spokesperson for the military’s special operations forces in West Kordofan, said in a Facebook post that the military was continuing to pursue the remaining RSF fighters of Group 302, led by Ali Balbla, along with RSF-aligned mobilized forces involved in the assault on Gabra al-Sheikh. A senior military officer told Mada Masr that Gabra al-Sheikh was the main operational objective of the RSF’s simultaneous escalation across several fronts in Sudan this week, which they described as a departure from the group’s better-known tactic of rapidly mobilizing forces for concentrated assaults on a single target. Retaking the area would allow the RSF to cut the Saderat Road, put pressure on the military and limit its ability to expand westward, the officer said. They described the fighting in North Kordofan as pivotal to the course of the war, with both sides treating the region as a decisive battlefield. On Thursday, the RSF also attacked Ayyara, located 40 km west of Obeid, North Kordofan’s capital. A field source from the mobilized civilians’ battalions fighting alongside the military said the RSF entered the area with more than 65 combat vehicles, but the attack was repelled and several vehicles were destroyed. *** After clashes inside Kauda, SPLM-N, Otoro fighting spreads to nearby villages Days after the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (Hilu) brought fighting with the Otoro tribe — one of its oldest constituencies — under control inside Kauda, the confrontation has spread to villages on the outskirts of the town, which serves as the movement’s political and military headquarters in South Kordofan. Fighting between the two sides broke out in several areas between Saturday and Monday, according to three sources from villages surrounding Kauda, with SPLM-N forces maintaining a heightened deployment around the town and tightening control over roads leading into it. The villages of Gardud and Hammam saw heavy artillery exchanges, driving dozens of families to flee toward Kubam and Kambra villages, the sources said. Many of these villages sit within corridors linking Kauda to the rural communities the town depends on for food, transport and supplies, according to a military source in SPLM-N factions that split from Hilu. Continued fighting there, the source said, weakens Kauda’s function as an administrative hub, even as the movement’s institutions inside the town itself remain under its control. Last week’s fighting inside Kauda marked the most dangerous escalation yet in a dispute that has been building since 2022, when SPLM-N moved to redraw administrative boundaries in areas under its control and redefine tribal landholdings across the Nuba Mountains. Many Otoro rejected the reform as an encroachment on ancestral land, and resistance eventually spread into the SPLM-N’s own army, where large numbers of Otoro serve. By March, the leadership was treating that resistance as mutiny, and in May it launched military operations in Otoro areas that left more than 60 people dead. Tensions continued to build over the following months, driven by broader Otoro demands for greater representation in the movement’s civilian and military institutions, until they reached SPLM-N’s own seat of power last week. For months now, people have lived under mounting pressure, the three villagers said, with civilian movement and market activity shifting from area to area depending on the security situation. In the words of the source who split from the Hilu faction, it is “a crisis with a moving geography.” Since last week’s escalation, SPLM-N forces deployed around Kauda are treating the area as a tightly controlled security zone, amid fears that fighting could return to the town itself, according to a resident of one of the nearby villages who is familiar with the security situation there. Checkpoints and stricter movement controls have become part of daily life, the source added, and families now weigh travel between villages as a security calculation rather than routine movement. What makes this confrontation harder to resolve, according to a former SPLM-N military source, is who the movement is up against. Unlike confrontations with external rivals, the source said, the SPLM-N faces groups with deep social and historical ties to its areas of influence and intimate knowledge of the local terrain and community networks, meaning military control alone will not be enough to end it. Continued military deployment may force SPLM-N to divert part of its forces and resources toward protecting key centers, roads and strategic sites within its territory, the source added, at a time when it is already under military pressure on other fronts, where it is fighting alongside the RSF against the Sudanese military. This does not necessarily mean the current confrontation threatens the movement’s military control over Kauda, but it does create an internal drain that becomes harder to ignore the longer the crisis continues, according to the source. Restoring calm, though, may be the easier part, according to a former South Kordofan State official who is also a notable of the Nuba peoples. The crisis confronts the movement’s leadership with something more complicated, requiring it to address the relationship between the central authority in Kauda and communities that feel their influence within the movement’s institutions has eroded in recent years. But SPLM-N leadership views the unification of administration and the building of centralized institutions as essential to holding its territories together, a source in SPLM-N told Mada Masr. Even so, the leadership is not blind to the cost. SPLM-N understands that the ongoing confrontation damages the image of the institutions it has built over years, a political source close to the movement said — particularly in Kauda, which stands as a model of local governance the movement has sought to present as an alternative to central state administration. Any long-term shift toward military administration in contested areas risks weakening that model and widening the distance between the institutions and the population, the source added. Both the Nuba notable and an Otoro notable see that continued military operations without addressing the community’s grievances will only produce new rounds of violence, even if the movement manages to impose a temporary calm in one area or another. This could, in the long term, harden into a recurring cycle: clashes in one area, followed by military buildup, followed by displacement and disrupted trade, followed by tension shifting elsewhere, the Nuba notable said. That scenario would put Kauda to a test that measures whether it can preserve its political centrality without that very centrality becoming a permanent source of conflict with everything around it, they added. To deflect such a scenario, the Otoro notable called for local negotiation channels to reopen, with native administrations and community leaders included in any new arrangements over land, security and governance. But while SPLM-N and tribal leaders weigh these long-term questions, people caught in the middle of it are contending with more immediate consequences. Security restrictions have disrupted markets, transportation and services, a field source working in relief operations in South Kordofan told Mada Masr. Residents have come to treat access to certain areas as contingent on the day’s fighting, driving up the cost of securing food and basic services, the source added. Humanitarian organizations, too, are running into obstacles reaching affected areas, the source continued. As the military footprint expands and checkpoints multiply, movement for aid workers and convoys grows more complicated, particularly in a region that relies on limited roads. No comprehensive independent figures yet exist on the scale of humanitarian need generated by the latest round of fighting, the source said, but displacement, market closures and disrupted transportation all point to an impact beyond the areas witnessing direct clashes. *** Kordofan governor in RSF-led govt defects Governor of the Kordofan region and member of the Tasis government’s presidential council Hamad Khalifa announces his defection from the RSF, August 12. Courtesy: Alhadath Alsudani Hamad Khalifa, the governor of the Kordofan region in the RSF-led Tasis government in western Sudan and a member of its presidential council, announced on Wednesday that he is defecting from the RSF, in the latest high-profile departure from the paramilitary group’s political and military camp. In a video interview with Al-Arabiya, Khalifa said he was resigning from his post, disavowing the RSF actions and abuses and calling on its members to return to the state. Khalifa’s departure is significant because of his position within a structure the RSF and its allies have sought to build to present their control over large parts of the country as an alternative political and administrative project, according to a former Sudanese intelligence official. When forming its presidential council in western Sudan last year, the RSF-led Tasis coalition divided Sudan into eight regions and appointed Khalifa governor of Kordofan and a member of the council. Khalifa had kept a low profile for several weeks and stopped attending presidential council meetings, according to a political source close to the Tasis leadership who spoke to Mada Masr. The source said he had left his residence under the pretext of routine administrative tours before announcing his resignation. According to a source close to Khalifa, his decision followed disagreements over the military situation and developments on the ground in his region. The source said he had objected to killings committed by the RSF and to drone attacks on Obeid, after Hemedti failed to heed his calls to rein in his forces. The departure has prompted increased scrutiny of administrative officials and executives working in RSF-controlled areas, according to a source close to Tasis’s political circles who spoke to Mada Masr. The source said regional governors have been instructed to obtain security clearance from the military leadership before moving. Khalifa’s departure follows a series of high-profile defections from the RSF in recent months. Al-Nour “Gubba” Adam, a former RSF commander in North Darfur and Mahamid tribal leader, defected earlier this year, with many of his fighters leaving Darfur with him. In May, former RSF field commander Ali “Savanna” Rizgallah also defected , followed in June by Fares al-Nour, a former close associate of Hemedti who handled sensitive political and diplomatic files. The series of departures do not signal an immediate military collapse of the RSF, a second source in Tasis’s political circles said. The group, they stressed, still has combat formations and the capability to retain control over large areas. For the former intelligence official, the significance of Khalifa’s departure lies in the fact that it adds an administrative dimension to the series of defections that involved military and political figures. Gubba and Savanna showed that field commanders could leave, while Fares al-Nour’s departure showed that Hemedti’s political circle was also susceptible, they said. According to the official, Khalifa’s exit now “puts Tasis’s regional face in question: what does the project look like on the ground if its own representatives begin to withdraw?” That does not amount to a comprehensive fragmentation of the RSF, the former official said. A more accurate description is a gradual fracturing across different levels of loyalty and representation, they added. *** Khartoum targets September for state-led political dialogue, preparations remain contested The intra-Sudanese political dialogue that Burhan has been preparing for months is now being targeted for a September launch, according to three political sources informed of the process and a source close to Burhan who spoke to Mada Masr, as the failure of international mediation in Addis Ababa has prompted a faster push on the domestic track. The government is now working to settle the dialogue’s preparatory arrangements, including who will sit on its preparatory committee, how participants will be selected and what issues will be addressed first, according to the sources. But these arrangements themselves remain contested, with the opposition Sumud coalition arguing that the forces expected to take part in the dialogue must have a say in the preparations, given that they will effectively determine the political process and its outcomes. Burhan had been laying the groundwork for the dialogue for months, consulting political forces, tribal leaders and national figures to build the political backing needed to launch it. But the pace picked up after another attempt to bring Sudan’s rival political camps together broke down in Addis Ababa in late July. The Quintet — comprising the African Union, United Nations, Arab League, European Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development — had convened the consultations to discuss a roadmap for a political process and the formation of a preparatory committee. The meetings failed to produce a joint discussion among the political forces. Instead, the Quintet held bilateral talks with several groups, particularly major blocs allied with the military, while the opposition Sumud coalition and the RSF-led Tasis stayed away. Both groups objected to how the Quintet is managing the mediation process and the selection of participating groups, with Sumud criticizing what it claimed was the Quintet’s insistence on including the former ruling National Congress Party, the Islamist current and affiliated groups. The coalition also objected to the prominent role given to parties aligned with the military-led government. The breakdown in Addis Ababa gave Sudan’s leadership an opening to move more quickly with its own track, a political source involved in the preparations said. September was subsequently set as the target for launching the dialogue inside Sudan. The government has taken cues from the disputes surrounding Addis Ababa. According to the source, the parties involved in the Burhan-led dialogue are seeking a formula that would prevent similar disagreements from derailing the process. For one, the National Congress Party would not take part in the dialogue, according to the source. There are also efforts to accommodate Sumud. More than 30 of its leaders face charges from the Sudanese government alleging that they undermined the constitutional order and rebelled against the state. The political source said efforts are underway to drop the cases, potentially clearing the way for the coalition to participate in the dialogue. But even if the legal issue is resolved, there is no clear agreement on the terms of Sumud’s participation. Bakry al-Jack, the coalition’s spokesperson, told Mada Masr that, in recent months, Sumud held contacts with figures and forces associated with the de facto authorities, but had received neither a formal or informal invitation to join a defined dialogue process. During those contacts, the coalition put forward its own sequencing of the political process, Jack said. Rather than moving directly into dialogue, it wants the process to begin with a cessation of fighting and measures to create a conducive humanitarian and political environment. Its proposal includes a three-month humanitarian truce, humanitarian corridors, guarantees for civilian protection, an end to weapons supplies to the warring parties and a freeze on administrative changes made during the war. The preparatory committee and political dialogue would come afterward. That puts what the political source described as the “pre-dialogue arrangements” at the center of the dispute. The immediate task for authorities now is to settle those arrangements, the political source said, but the substance of what needs to be settled remains contentious. One of the key issues is the composition of the preparatory committee, according to a second source informed of the consultations. The committee would set the format and agenda of the conference and communicate with political and civil forces and establish the rules for participation. Discussions are still focused on its size and selection, including whether the main political blocs should be represented equally or whether other civilian and community-based forces should be brought in. The stakes are high because the committee would, in practice, determine who gets a seat at the dialogue table. According to Jack, Sumud argues that the arrangements for the dialogue, including the committee formation, should themselves be negotiated, rather than determined in advance and presented to the participating forces as a finished process. That is significant because the government’s “pre-dialogue arrangements” already include a work plan, an initial outline of the agenda, according to the source close to Burhan, even though the preparatory committee would later be tasked with organizing and developing it. The agenda is contentious in part because the government and war opponents do not share the same starting point. Burhan sees the dialogue as a vehicle for rebuilding state institutions and setting the terms for the next phase, with the military-led authorities retaining control over the process. Forces opposed to the war, by contrast, want the fighting to end and a political and humanitarian environment to be established before questions about political power and the future shape of the state are taken up. The government is seeking to move toward its end point in stages, rather than convening a single, unwieldy conference expected to settle every issue at once, a third political source said. The proposed process would begin with a preparatory phase, followed by political sessions, and then discussions on the transitional period and rebuilding state institutions. The preparatory committee would determine how issues are prioritized and when they are brought into the process, the source said. That makes both the committee’s composition and the work plan already taking shape consequential for parties looking to secure a place in the process. If the initial outline sets the direction of the dialogue, the committee could have limited room to alter it, and whoever controls its membership will ultimately have a say in determining which issues receive priority. Excluding a political force from the preparatory phase thus would effectively exclude it from shaping the rules of the dialogue and eventually its outcomes. Contacts will continue in the coming period as the parties try to settle the formula before September, with both the participant list and the preparatory committee still unresolved, according to the three political sources. *** Back-to-back Sudanese visits to Juba in mutual push to contain border, Abyei tensions Sudanese Defense Minister Hassan Kabron and his South Sudanese counterpart Chol Thon Balok meet at the Ministry of Defence and Veterans Affairs headquarters in Juba, August 10. Courtesy: The Sudanese Defense Ministry A month of high-level maneuvering around Khartoum-Juba relations continued this week, with two back-to-back visits to the South Sudanese capital — Sudanese Defense Minister Hassan Kabron on Sunday, followed a day later by Darfur Governor Minni Arko Minnawi. Kabron led a senior military and security delegation into talks with his South Sudanese counterpart. The next day, Minnawi held meetings with Tut Gatluak, the security affairs advisor to President Salva Kiir. The shared border and the armed groups moving across it dominated both sets of talks, alongside the disputed Abyei territory and the protection of oil interests on both sides of the border. The flurry of activity follows South Sudan’s mid-July announcement that stirred formal protest in Khartoum: Abyei, unresolved between the two states since the 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement, would be folded into the electoral districts for the country’s first general elections, scheduled for December. Simultaneously, Sudan’s military has been pushing deeper into Kordofan — the oil-rich region bordering South Sudan that carries the infrastructure piping South Sudanese oil through Sudan for export — with vows to keep advancing toward Darfur. The two delegations’ visits to Juba came as an attempt to reopen a direct channel with Sudan’s military leadership, a Sudanese diplomatic source said, at a moment when South Sudan’s approaching political and electoral milestones make it all the more important for Juba to keep its northern border out of the escalation. That border carries particular weight given the fighting underway in Sudan, where the military is trying to sever the RSF’s supply lines from Ethiopia, Libya and Chad — potentially leaving South Sudan’s northern border as the RSF’s last remaining resupply route, according to the source. The visits also pave the way for Burhan’s own trip to Juba soon, the source added. In a visit to Khartoum in late July, Gatluak delivered a written message from Kiir to Burhan inviting him to a bilateral summit in Juba in the coming weeks, with the agenda covering a range of unresolved issues — Abyei, border demarcation and stalled security and economic arrangements among them, according to a Sudanese diplomatic source who spoke to Mada Masr at the time Border control was the focus of Kabron’s own talks in Juba, including blocking the movement of armed groups, protecting oil facilities and pipelines and discussing temporary security arrangements to contain tensions around Abyei, according to a South Sudanese source informed of the visit. Minnawi’s talks covered much the same topics. A Sudanese diplomatic source informed of the trip told Mada Masr that the visit focused on the Abyei file, the war’s impact on the Sudan-South Sudan border and the movement of armed forces and groups across it. The meeting also discussed political and security contacts with South Sudanese officials, the source added, at a moment when Juba’s role in southern and western Sudan’s security arrangements is growing. Khartoum can treat Abyei as an open negotiating issue, a former senior Sudanese diplomat familiar with the file said. But it struggles with South Sudanese measures that create new administrative and political facts on the ground in the disputed area — one of the factors, the diplomat added, that has accelerated security contacts between the two countries. The concern is that political disputes could turn into friction on the ground, particularly given the area’s history of tension between the Ngok Dinka and the Misseria tribes, seasonal herder movements across the border and fragile security arrangements. Sensitivities in Abyei have doubled since the Sudan war broke out, an official in the territory said. Large numbers of displaced people have flowed into the area, straining resources, services and traditional grazing routes, while the area itself has grown more exposed to the fallout of military operations on the Sudanese side of the border. The UN’s interim security force for Abyei, UNISFA, continues to monitor military movements and local tensions, the source said. “The presence of armed forces and armed groups around Abyei adds to the complexity,” the official said. “The further the Sudanese war extends south and west, the more important these border areas become as movement and supply lines. Juba is trying to stop its border with Sudan from turning into an open corridor for fighters and weapons.” Oil is central to these calculations. South Sudan relies almost entirely on Sudanese infrastructure to move its crude through Sudanese territory to Red Sea ports. Khartoum, in turn, collects transit fees that count among the few revenue sources it has left amid the war. That makes the Heglig oil fields, pipelines and related facilities in West Kordofan, bordering Abyei, a shared national security concern. Any major disruption to production or transport areas would carry a direct cost for Juba’s economy and for public finances in Khartoum. Juba is keen to keep the political dispute over Abyei separate from the economic interests tied to oil, a South Sudanese official informed of the file said. The South Sudanese government recognizes a major security escalation on the border would hurt both sides. Kiir’s government still faces domestic pressure on the issue, though, from political forces and local communities who feel the Abyei file has been left hanging too long and want steps taken to affirm the territory’s ties to South Sudan, according to the source. A senior South Sudanese government official described Gatluak’s visit to Khartoum and Kabron’s visit to Juba as reflecting both sides’ wish to build a more regular security channel. Ugandan contacts with Khartoum over South Sudan in recent weeks add a regional layer to these arrangements, the official said. Kampala’s involvement carries particular weight given its place in the web of security and political relationships surrounding the Sudanese war, and its direct ties to the South Sudan file. The old bilateral mechanisms can no longer keep pace with the new realities Sudan’s war has created, another Sudanese diplomat said, and the two states are now seeking direct lines of contact between their military and security bodies instead. The real test of these contacts, the diplomat added, will come in Abyei more than in any other file, since any friction there could quickly escalate into a crisis between the two states, especially with South Sudan’s elections drawing near. *** Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . The post Sudan Nashra: In cross-border offensive, RSF seizes Blue Nile’s Geisan, recaptures Kurmuk | Military repels major RSF attack on North Kordofan’s Gabra al-Sheikh | After clashes inside Kauda, SPLM-N-Otoro fighting spreads to nearby villages | Kordofan governor in RSF-led govt defects | Back-to-back Sudanese visits to Juba in mutual push to contain border, Abyei tensions first appeared on Mada Masr .

items.title: Des vivres et non-vivres aux victimes des inondations
items.description: Tabligbo, 14 août (ATOP) – Soixante-cinq ménages victimes des inondations des pluies diluviennes du 28 juin dernier dans les localités de Essè-Godjin, Akladjénou, Atakpamédé et de Gboto-Klohomé dans la commune Yoto 3 ont bénéficié de kits de vivres et non-vivres, le jeudi 13 août dans leurs localités respectives. Chaque ménage a reçu un kit composé notamment d’un sac de riz de 25kg, d’un bidon d’huile de 3 litres, des ustensiles de cuisine. Deux seaux en plastique, deux couvertures épaisses de deux places, deux nattes, cinq pièces de savons, deux sacs de conditionnement. L’ONG Plan international-Togo, à travers cette action, entend apporter un soutien aux ménages touchés. Il s’agit aussi de renforcer leur capacité à faire face aux difficultés engendrées par le sinistre. Un lot des kits A l’occasion, l’assistance a été sensibilisée sur la gestion des risques liées aux catastrophes et la politique de sauvegarde de Plan international Togo. Les échanges ont permis de rappeler aux bénéficiaires les comportements à adopter face aux risques et les mécanismes de protection mis en place par l’organisation. Dans le souci de renforcer la prise en compte des préoccupations des bénéficiaires, un comité de veille de trois membres a été mis en place. Il aura notamment pour mission de recueillir les plaintes et préoccupations liées à l’intervention. Le directeur de la mise en œuvre des programmes de Plan international Togo, Soba Palakeyém a expliqué la stratégie mise en place par l’organisation pour répondre aux besoins des victimes. Il a également appelé les populations à davantage de prudence dans le choix des sites de construction, notamment en évitant les zones marécageuses et les lits des cours d’eau. Le coordinateur des programmes de Plan international dans la région Maritime et des Plateaux, Tsigbé Kodjo a précisé que les kits distribués constituent un premier secours en attendant la mobilisation d’autres moyens pour répondre durablement aux besoins des ménages affectés. Il les a invités à prendre soin des kits. Les bénéficiaires ont exprimé leur remerciement aux donateurs pour cette action humanitaire et de générosité. La remise s’est déroulée en présence des autorités locales, des chefs de services, des représentants de l’Agence nationale de la protection civile (ANPC) et du ministère en charge des Solidarités ainsi que des responsables des forces de défense et de sécurité. ATOP/SAK/MG/BV

items.title: Bassar / Télécommunications : Les consommateurs sensibilisés sur leurs droits et obligations
items.description: Bassar, 14 août (ATOP) – Les membres des associations de consommateurs et des représentants des populations de Mô, Bassar et Dankpen ont été sensibilisés sur leurs droits, leurs obligations et les bonnes pratiques liées à l’utilisation des services de téléphonie mobile, le jeudi 13 août à Bassar. La rencontre a été initiée par l’Autorité de régulation des communications électroniques et des postes (ARCEP), avec l’appui financier et technique de Moov Africa Togo. Elle s’inscrit dans le cadre d’une tournée nationale d’information et de sensibilisation, prévue du 3 au 28 août, sous le thème : « L’ARCEP à l’écoute des consommateurs des services de communications électroniques et des postes ». L’objectif est de renforcer les connaissances des consommateurs sur les services proposés par les opérateurs de communications électroniques, leurs droits et les mécanismes de recours en cas de difficultés. L’initiative vise également à mieux faire connaître les moyens de prévention contre les arnaques ainsi que les procédures de saisine de l’ARCEP en cas de plainte ou de réclamation. Séance d’information et de sensibilisation Les échanges ont porté sur la protection des usagers des services de téléphonie, la sécurité liée aux infrastructures et aux antennes des réseaux radioélectriques, ainsi que la prévention des fraudes liées aux services de monnaie électronique, notamment Moov Money. Les participants ont également été informés des démarches à suivre pour introduire une réclamation auprès des opérateurs. Le directeur juridique et de la protection des consommateurs à l’ARCEP, Kader Ouro-Agoro, a invité les participants à servir de relais dans leurs communautés respectives afin de partager les informations reçues. « Tout citoyen résidant sur le territoire national doit bénéficier des mêmes services que ceux qui sont dans les grandes villes », a-t-il souligné. Il a également appelé les usagers à davantage de vigilance face aux tentatives d’arnaque et d’escroquerie, assurant que leurs réclamations et suggestions seront prises en compte dans l’amélioration des services. Le responsable des enquêtes et investigations de la Ligue des consommateurs du Togo (LCT), Bright Fiaga, représentant les associations de consommateurs, a rappelé que les usagers ont le droit de réclamer en cas de difficultés liées à leurs forfaits d’appels, aux services internet, au Cash Power ou à la qualité du réseau téléphonique. Il les a invités à partager les informations reçues avec leurs communautés, en rappelant que le numéro vert gratuit 8000 est disponible pour toute dénonciation, réclamation ou demande d’accompagnement. Le maire de la commune Bassar 1, Mouni Ouyi, ainsi que des représentants des organisations et associations de consommateurs ont pris part à la rencontre. ATOP/LK/AO/KYA

items.title: Ebola en RDC: une sixième province touchée, l’OMS renforce la riposte régionale
items.description: Une sixième province de la République démocratique du Congo (RDC) est désormais touchée par l’épidémie de maladie à virus Ebola. La détection d’un cas mortel dans le Bas-Uele, frontalier de la Centrafrique, intervient alors que l’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS) réunit à Bangui les autorités sanitaires de cinq pays voisins pour renforcer la coordination transfrontalière et prévenir une propagation régionale du virus. La détection d’un décès lié au virus Ebola de type Bundibugyo dans le Bas-Uele marque une nouvelle étape dans l’évolution de l’épidémie. Jusqu’ici épargnée, cette province septentrionale partage une frontière avec la République centrafricaine (RCA). Selon l’agence sanitaire de l’Union africaine, CDC Afrique, la personne décédée aurait voyagé depuis la province du Haut-Uele, déjà touché par l’épidémie. Avec cette nouvelle province affectée, six provinces de la RDC sont désormais concernées : le Bas-Uele, l’Ituri, le Nord-Kivu, le Sud-Kivu, le Haut-Uele et la Tshopo. Buta, 54e zone de santé touchée Selon les autorités sanitaires congolaises, la zone de santé de Buta, dans le Bas-Uele, est désormais la 54e zone de santé affectée par l’épidémie. Le dernier rapport de situation fait état de 4.665 cas confirmés, dont 2.184 décès, depuis la déclaration de l’épidémie en mai. Au total, 965 personnes ont été guéries. L’Ituri demeure l’épicentre de l’épidémie. Le taux de létalité s’établit à 46 %, tandis que le taux de suivi des contacts atteint 84 %. C’est dans ce contexte que le directeur régional de l’OMS pour l’Afrique, Mohamed Janabi, est arrivé jeudi dans la capitale centrafricaine Bangui. Il participe vendredi à une réunion de haut niveau de deux jours consacrée au virus Bundibugyo, avec les autorités sanitaires de la Centrafrique, de la RDC, de l’Ouganda, du Soudan du Sud et de la République du Congo. Les frontières au cœur de la riposte À Bangui, l’objectif est de renforcer la coordination entre les pays, d’identifier les failles aux frontières et d’anticiper toute nouvelle transmission. « Il faut une collaboration transfrontalière solide pour empêcher toute propagation supplémentaire et éviter une crise sanitaire régionale de plus grande ampleur », estime le responsable de l’OMS. L’enjeu dépasse toutefois la seule coordination entre services de santé. La proximité des zones affectées avec plusieurs pays voisins fait craindre une propagation du virus au-delà des frontières congolaises. « Et ici, nous sommes confrontés à une épidémie de choléra. De l’autre côté, ils ont Bundibugyo. Donc, si nous ne protégeons pas la République centrafricaine, il y a un risque que l’épidémie se propage jusqu’ici et qu’elle atteigne également Kinshasa, qui est une grande ville ; c’est un risque que nous devons tous prendre en compte », a insisté le chef du bureau régional de l’OMS pour l’Afrique. Face à un virus qui ne s’arrête pas aux frontières, l’OMS plaide pour une réponse coordonnée : partage d’expertise, surveillance conjointe, échange d’informations et renforcement des partenariats doivent permettre de détecter rapidement les cas et de limiter les risques de transmission. Cette coopération est d’autant plus importante que l’incidence reste élevée dans l’est de la RDC, notamment le long des principaux axes de déplacement vers l’Ouganda et le Soudan du Sud. Surveiller les couloirs de mobilité à haut risque Sur le terrain, la surveillance se poursuit aux points d’entrée et aux points de contrôle situés le long des principaux couloirs de mobilité, malgré des contraintes opérationnelles persistantes sur certains sites. Pour l’OMS, il est essentiel de renforcer encore la surveillance transfrontalière et le partage d’informations afin de permettre une détection précoce et une prise en charge rapide de toute transmission au-delà des frontières. À Bangui, les responsables sanitaires des cinq pays voisins de la RDC doivent notamment « tirer les leçons de l’expérience ougandaise, comprendre ce qui se passe actuellement en République démocratique du Congo, et que la mesure la plus importante pour prévenir la propagation est de renforcer la frontière ». Le dernier rapport épidémiologique de l’OMS identifie plusieurs priorités : renforcer la surveillance le long des couloirs de mobilité transfrontaliers à haut risque, y compris les passages informels, développer la surveillance événementielle et la recherche active de cas, et assurer le partage d’informations en temps réel grâce à des réunions régulières de coordination entre pays. Pour l’OMS, l’objectif est désormais d’empêcher que la progression de l’épidémie en RDC ne se transforme en crise sanitaire régionale. Source: ONU Infos L’article Ebola en RDC: une sixième province touchée, l’OMS renforce la riposte régionale est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Non, le lac de Côme en Italie ne s’est pas vidé
items.description: Le lac de Côme au nord de l’Italie aurait disparu à la suite d’une “rupture géologique”, annonce un reportage diffusé sur TikTok. C’est inexact : d’une part, les images de ce reportage ont été générées par intelligence artificielle. D’autre part, si le niveau du lac a effectivement baissé c’est-à-cause de la sécheresse, et les images satellites montrent que le lac de Côme est encore loin d’être tari.

items.title: Des veuves de la commune wawa1 bénéficient de 3000 plants de cacao
items.description: Badou, 14 août (ATOP) – Les lauréats de prix d’excellence du cacao de la préfecture de Wawa ont offert 3000 plants de cacao et 300 plants d’ombrage à 10 femmes veuves de la commune Wawa1, le vendredi 14 août, à Tomégbé, à 10 km au sud de Badou. Cette initiative vise à promouvoir l’excellence dans la production cacaoyère au sein de la préfecture et à contribuer au développement harmonieux et durable de la filière. Il s’agit d’améliorer considérablement les revenus des femmes bénéficiaires dans leurs différentes localités d’ici à 3 ans. Chaque bénéficiaire a reçu au total 300 plants de cacao et 30 plants d’ombrages. Ces plants couvriront une superficie de 0, 25 hectares de plantation. Les bénéficiaires ont été renseignées sur le processus d’installation d’une nouvelle plantation de cacao et sur l’itinéraire technique à suivre pour de meilleurs rendements après 3 ans d’entretien et de bonnes pratiques agraires. Le porte-parole des lauréats M. Toulassi Kokou a indiqué que la culture du cacao est une école de patience, de durs labeurs et de dignité. « Nous nous engageons avec l’appui des techniciens de l’UTCC de la zone Wawa à accompagner les bénéficiaires pour la mise en terre de ces plants, leur entretien et les bonnes pratiques agricoles à travers un suivi régulier » a-t-il indiqué. La porte-parole des bénéficiaires Mme Goka Akossiwa, a au nom des bénéficiaires remercié les donateurs pour cette marque de solidarité et de sympathie à leur égard. « Nous promettons utiliser les plants de cacao offerts à bon escient afin d’atteindre les objectifs fixés par les donateurs et jouir d’une autonomie financière à la fin » a-t-elle indiqué Cette cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence du technicien de l’ICAT Koyawo Kokou qui a promis soutenir et faire un suivi régulier des plantations des bénéficiaires durant les trois prochaines années pour de résultats probants. ATOP/PM/KKT/KYA

items.title: Yann Vézilier gracié : vers un rapprochement entre Bamako et Paris ?
items.description: La grâce presidentielle accordee a Yann Vezilier, « agent des services de renseignements francais », suscite des reactions au sein de l'opinion publique malienne. Certains y voient un geste susceptible de favoriser l'apaisement et la reprise du dialogue entre Bamako et Paris. D'autres estiment que cette decision ne suffit pas, a elle seule, a normaliser les relations entre les deux pays. a Bamako comme a l'interieur du pays, la mesure de grâce accordee a Yann Vezilier est accueillie avec des reactions differentes. « ca montre que notre president pense reellement au pays. Mais ce n'est pas pour autant que ca veut dire qu'avec la France on va reprendre les relations qu'on avait auparavant », nous confie une dame que nous avons croisee en circulation a Badalabougou (Bamako). a Yirimadio, un autre habitant de la capitale estime que la decision merite d'etre saluee : « C'est evident d'applaudir cette initiative prise par les hautes autorites maliennes ». a Yanfolila, dans la region de Bougouni, un autre citoyen considere egalement cette grâce comme une decision positive. « On ne connaît pas les coulisses mais si c'est une decision presidentielle de le gracier, je pense que c'est une bonne chose. Je pense bien que ca peut etre le debut d'une bonne reconciliation entre les deux Etats. » Un possible signal d'apaisement Au-dela des reactions citoyennes, cette decision est egalement analysee comme un eventuel signal d'apaisement dans les relations entre le Mali et la France. Pour l'universitaire Pierre-Claver Bakoroba Traore, il est toutefois premature de parler de normalisation. « Normalisation, peut-etre pas vraiment, mais apaisement, oui. » Selon lui, les deux pays ont aujourd'hui interet a tourner la page. « Plus d'une fois les autorites francaises avaient exprime le vœu que leur citoyen soit libere. Donc dans ce sens, je dirai que ca peut apporter un apaisement. » Quelle suite pour les relations Mali-France ? La grâce presidentielle accordee a Yann Vezilier peut ainsi etre interpretee comme un geste susceptible de contribuer a l'apaisement entre Bamako et Paris. Mais son impact sur les relations bilaterales reste a mesurer. a noter que cette mesure de grâce est intervenue seulement quelques minutes apres l'annonce de la liberation de 82 militaires maliens par les groupes armes. Un rapprochement qui alimente les interrogations au sein de l'opinion. L’article Yann Vézilier gracié : vers un rapprochement entre Bamako et Paris ? est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: Kéran/ santé publique : Des acteurs du district préfectoral s’imprègnent de l’approche ‘’7-1-7’’
items.description: Kantè, 14 août (ATOP) – Les acteurs du district sanitaire de la Kéran se sont imprégnés, le vendredi 14 août à Kantè, de l’approche ‘’7-1-7’’. Cette formation est organisée par la direction régionale de la Santé de la Kara en collaboration avec l’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS). L’objectif est de renforcer les capacités des acteurs de surveillance, notamment les membres des équipes cadres et les responsables des formations sanitaires du district préfectoral de la Kéran, sur les différents aspects de cette approche. Il s’agit également de doter les bénéficiaires de cette formation d’outils nécessaires dans la mise en œuvre de ladite approche, en assurant une riposte efficace des épidémies et des évènements de santé publique. Les modules de la formation portent notamment sur la revue précoce des premières actions de l’OMS. Ces communications ont été suivies de témoignage sur la gestion d’une épidémie dans le district de la Kéran (exemple de l’épidémie de la fièvre typhoïde) ainsi que de la réflexion sur la base de gestion de l’épidémie et l’approche ‘’7-1-7’’. L’approche ‘’7-1-7’’ permet d’identifier et de corriger en temps réel par un coût minime ou gratuit, les problèmes et les goulots d’étranglement ayant été négligés lors d’évaluations précédentes. Elle a été adoptée par le bureau régional de l’OMS pour l’Afrique dans le cadre de sa stratégie régionale pour la sécurité sanitaire et les situations d’urgence 2022-2030. Les résultats des projets pilotes ont démontré que l’approche ‘’7-1-7’’ est réalisable dans divers pays à revenu élevé, intermédiaire ou faible, afin d’améliorer les performances du système de sécurité sanitaire, en répondant efficacement aux épidémies. La cérémonie a été présidée par le médecin lieutenant-Colonel Kotosso Awèréou, directeur régional du Centre des maladies infectieuses de la Kara en présence du chargé ‘’Préparation aux urgences’’ à l’OMS-Togo, Dr Alassani Issifou, et du représentant du directeur préfectoral de la Santé de la Kéran, Tchangaï Patoki. ATOP/PAP/AR/KYA

items.title: Burkina : l’entreprise Elite Digital lance la plateforme « Songré » pour rapprocher les services numériques des populations
items.description: Burkina-Technologie- Songré-Lancement Burkina : l’entreprise Elite Digital lance la plateforme « Songré » pour rapprocher les services numériques des populations Ouagadougou, 14 août 2026 (AIB)-Le promoteur de l’entreprise Elite Digital, une agence spécialisée dans le SMS marketing et les solutions numériques, Abdou Yougbaré a lancé, vendredi à Ouagadougou, la plateforme numérique « Songré », destinée à faciliter la vie quotidienne des Burkinabè à travers plusieurs services sécurisés. « Songré », en langue mooré, qui signifie «aide » n’est pas qu’une application mobile. C’est une plateforme pensée pour simplifier la vie, rapprocher les acteurs et sécuriser les interactions », a déclaré le promoteur, Abdou Yougbaré. Selon lui, la plateforme doit notamment servir de pont entre les étudiants et les entreprises, en facilitant l’accès aux stages et aux opportunités professionnelles. Elle intègre un service de géolocalisation destiné à permettre aux utilisateurs de trouver rapidement une pharmacie de garde ou un centre de santé. Elle propose également une « Marketplace sécurisée, où la confiance n’est plus une option, mais une garantie, ainsi qu’un service de coursiers moderne pour alléger le quotidien et optimiser le temps de chacun », a poursuivi Yougbaré Abdou. Le promoteur d’Elite Digital a expliqué que « Songré » ambitionne de contribuer à la réduction du chômage des jeunes, de dynamiser le commerce local et de renforcer la confiance dans les échanges économiques. La plateforme vise également à rapprocher les services essentiels des populations. Selon le partenaire stratégique de « Songré », Hugues Gouba, beaucoup de personnes sont victimes d’arnaques sur les réseaux sociaux après avoir commandé des produits en ligne, qui se révèlent parfois défectueux. Aujourd’hui, avec « cet outil polyvalent » vous êtes sûr de passer par une plateforme sérieuse et aussi un vendeur sérieux », a rassuré le partenaire stratégique, ajoutant qu’elle n’est pas seulement une application mais une réponse concrète à des besoins réels de la société. Yougbaré Abdou et Hugues Gouba ont invité les entreprises, les étudiants, les commerçants et l’ensemble des citoyens à s’approprier cet outil, indiquant qu’une innovation n’a de valeur que si elle est utilisée. Agence d’information du Burkina OB/yos

items.title: Transhumance à Gaya : agriculteurs et éleveurs face aux défis du partage des ressources
items.description: Listen to « Transhumance a Gaya : agriculteurs et eleveurs face aux defis du partage des ressources (Forum) » on Spreaker. Situee a la frontiere entre le Niger et le Benin, la zone de Gaya constitue un important corridor de transhumance. Chaque annee, des milliers de tetes de betail y transitent a la recherche de pâturages et de points d'eau. Le forum s'interesse aux difficultes liees a cette mobilite pastorale et aux pistes de solution. Parmi les defis evoques figurent la reduction des espaces de pâturage, l'occupation des couloirs de transhumance par les activites agricoles, le manque de points d'eau, les effets du changement climatique, l'insecurite, les controles administratifs et les difficultes de franchissement des frontieres. Les conflits entre agriculteurs et eleveurs constituent egalement une preoccupation. Le passage des troupeaux dans les champs peut occasionner des degâts sur les cultures et provoquer des tensions. Les echanges portent sur le fonctionnement des couloirs de passage, le respect des itineraires officiels, les mecanismes de reglement des differends et les effets de la pression sur les terres. Invites : • Lawali Ibrahim, secretaire general de la COFOCOM au niveau departemental ; • Elhadji Souley, president de Finan Daddo et representant des eleveurs ; • Nassirou Mahamane, cultivateur. Moderation : Ramatou Issa Ouanke. Photo par Vincent van Zeijst – Source : Wikipedia – CC BY-SA 4.0

items.title: Burkina : L’ADCT comptabilise plus de 18 000 réalisations au profit des collectivités territoriales
items.description: En prélude à la caravane de presse consacrée à la valorisation de ses interventions au profit des collectivités territoriales du Burkina Faso, l’Agence nationale d’appui au développement des collectivités territoriales (ADCT) a organisé, ce vendredi 14 août 2026, un atelier d’immersion au profit des professionnels des médias. Cette rencontre visait à renforcer la compréhension des journalistes en ce qui concerne les missions, l’organisation et les mécanismes d’intervention de l’ADCT. « Pour mieux rendre compte de l’action publique, il faut d’abord mieux la comprendre », cette phrase de Daouda Guiro, représentant la Directrice générale de l’ADCT, résume tout l'objet de cet atelier. Et pour permettre a la dizaine d'hommes et femmes de médias présents, trois communications ont été animées. La première, présentée par Daouda Guiro, Directeur des affaires juridiques, a porté sur le cadre juridique des interventions de l’ADCT. Dans sa communication, M. Guiro a souligné que le Fonds permanent, créé en 2004 par la loi portant Code général des collectivités territoriales, a progressivement évolué pour donner naissance à l’ADCT en 2007. Daouda Guiro, représentant la Directrice générale, et communicant sur le cadre juridique de l'ADCT Sa communication a également permis de revenir sur les deux principales fonctions de l’Agence dans l’accompagnement des collectivités territoriales à savoir l’appui financier et l’appui technique. « L’appui financier s’effectue à travers différents guichets, dont le guichet des fonds fongibles, le guichet de la dotation spéciale et les prêts. L’appui technique, quant à lui, se matérialise par l’accompagnement à la maîtrise d’ouvrage et à la maîtrise d’œuvre, le renforcement des capacités des collectivités ainsi que la mise à leur disposition d’une banque d’outils.», a-t-il expliqué. Par ailleurs, Daouda Guiro a évoqué plusieurs défis auxquels l’Agence entend apporter des réponses, notamment l’accréditation au Fonds vert pour le climat afin de faciliter l’accès aux financements climatiques, ainsi que de l’octroi de 100 bourses à des fonctionnaires des collectivités territoriales pour leur formation à l’Ecole nationale d'administration et de magistrature (ENAM). Des interventions organisées autour de plusieurs guichets Le mode opératoire de l’ADCT a ensuite été présenté par Léonce Yao, Directeur des opérations de financement. Il a rappelé que les interventions de l’Agence couvrent notamment la préparation des projets, la maîtrise d’ouvrage et le suivi, le renforcement des capacités ainsi que l’appui institutionnel. Ces interventions sont organisées autour de six guichets, dont cinq sont actuellement fonctionnels.L’ensemble des collectivités territoriales constitue le public bénéficiaire. Léonce Yao, Directeur des opérations de financement « Dans la répartition des financements, plusieurs principes encadrent les interventions de l’ADCT, notamment l’équité, la solidarité, la transparence, la mutabilité et l’intangibilité de la maîtrise d’ouvrage.» a-t-il signifié. Face aux conséquences de la crise sécuritaire, l’Agence a également œuvré à la stabilisation et au relèvement des collectivités territoriales affectées, tout en poursuivant l’accompagnement à la réalisation de projets locaux. Plus de 18 000 réalisations enregistrées depuis 2008 La dernière communication, consacrée aux acquis et aux perspectives de l’ADCT, a été animée par Sibiri Jacques Kaboré, chargé d’appui technique. Selon lui, l’Agence mobilise en moyenne 10 milliards de francs CFA au profit des collectivités territoriales. « De 2008 à nos jours, 18 projets et programmes ont été mis en œuvre, avec 18 437 réalisations dans six secteurs clés » , a-t-il indiqué citant le secteur de l’éducation, celui l’hygiène, de la santé, du climat et du développement socio-économique. Sibiri Jacques Kaboré, chargé d'appui technique à l'ADCT Parmi les principaux acquis, il a relevé l’amélioration de la performance institutionnelle, la mobilisation et la pérennisation des ressources, l’opérationnalisation du mécanisme unifié de financement des collectivités territoriales, ainsi que la conformité aux orientations de la Réforme de la politique publique (RPP). L’ADCT entend en outre, selon Sibiri Kaboré, renforcer son positionnement auprès des institutions de financement des collectivités territoriales de l’Alliance des États du Sahel (AES). Pour les prochaines années, les perspectives portent notamment sur le renforcement de la performance institutionnelle et l’optimisation de la mobilisation des ressources. À travers cet atelier d’immersion, l’ADCT entend ainsi donner aux professionnels des médias les clés nécessaires pour mieux comprendre et valoriser les actions menées au bénéfice des collectivités territoriales. Une démarche qui ouvre la voie à la caravane de presse, au cours de laquelle les journalistes pourront aller à la rencontre des réalisations concrètes de l’Agence sur le terrain. Sidziguin Irène Corinne SAWADOGO (Stagiaire) Minute.bf

items.title: 1ère édition de « la nuit des femmes des médias » : L’AFPM-Togo met en lumière le leadership féminin
items.description: Lomé, 14 août (ATOP) – Seulement 19,2 % des femmes sont à la tête des médias au Togo. Ce chiffre a été révélé par la présidente de l’Association des femmes professionnelles des médias du Togo (AFPM-Togo), Mme Élisabeth Apampa, lors du lancement de la 1 ère édition de « La Nuit des femmes des médias », le vendredi 14 août à Lomé. Cet événement a pour thème : « Sensibiliser, informer, agir pour le développement durable ». Il a pour objectif de permettre aux femmes de se rencontrer, de se connaître et de co-construire ensemble des initiatives à impact. La rencontre vise à démontrer que les femmes des médias contribuent, par leur voix et leur engagement, à faire avancer les Objectifs de développement durable (ODD), notamment l’ODD 5 consacré à l’égalité entre les sexes. Deux activités sont inscrites au programme. Dans la journée, la première dénommée « Le village des médias » a été consacrée à un panel de discussion sur le thème retenu. Outre ce thème, la thématique du harcèlement en milieu professionnel a été abordée. La seconde activité, « la nuit des femmes des médias » servira de cadre de réseautage conçu pour favoriser le partage et la co-construction d’initiatives à fort impact. Le panel de discussion Mme Apampa a indiqué que « Le village des médias » est une manière de montrer que tous les médias ont une facilité de se déplacer et d’être dans la proximité. « Nous aurons ici, juste après ce panel, des émissions en direct qui vont se dérouler. Et ensuite, vous allez échanger avec ces médias qui sont déjà positionnés pour vous parler de ce qu’ils proposent. Parce que le travail, c’est de montrer que même si le média est porté par un homme, au sein de l’organe, il y a des femmes tapies dans l’ombre, qui font des choses merveilleuses, pas forcément à l’écran », a déclaré la présidente de l’AFPM-Togo. La présidente de AFPM-Togo a invité les femmes à dénoncer tout harcèlement en milieu professionnel. « Quand tu vis le harcèlement, quand tu discutes avec ta collègue, ce n’est pas une dénonciation. Donc, il faut aller au-delà du partage d’expériences, mais dénoncer, parce que la loi nous protège. Il y a des mécanismes juridiques aujourd’hui qui existent au Togo. Le Togo est vraiment dans un progrès énorme pour protéger les femmes. C’est à nous de nous saisir de ces textes-là pour nous protéger », a-t-elle souligné. Le directeur de cabinet de la Haute autorité de régulation de la communication écrite, audiovisuelle et numérique (HARC), Abarim Olivier Yao, a rappelé qu’il existe plusieurs textes juridiques qui protègent les femmes, notamment le code de la presse. Il a invité les femmes à se positionner et, au-delà du positionnement, à se former afin d’être davantage propulsées aux postes de responsabilité. La rencontre s’est déroulée en présence des représentants du ministère de la Communication, des membres de l’AFPM-Togo ainsi que des journalistes. ATOP/MD/SED/KYA
